docs.title: GlassOps™
docs.text: Governance-first Salesforce DevOps.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
GlassOps is a CI-agnostic command line tool that acts as the CI/CD layer for Salesforce delivery, with other platforms possible later. It is written in Go and replaces the older GitHub Action runtime that this repository once held.

The current release is v1.1.0. It adds opt-in Sigstore signing, Rego rules, a pull request comment and OpenTelemetry export. v1.0.0 was the first final release. All releases are on the releases page. GlassOps has deployed a real Salesforce project to production through its full deploy pipeline: plan, validate, gate, deploy, verify and report, in a protected GitHub environment. What is in which release lists every command and feature with the release that first has it.

docs.title: The glassops CLI
docs.text:
The CLI lives at the repository root (cmd/, internal/, schemas/). Each step is its own command, and glassops run runs a whole pipeline of them. Salesforce is the built-in provider, and provider exec runs your own commands for any other deploy tool. The CI layers are GitHub Actions, Bitbucket Pipelines and GitLab CI. The last two have not run on a real runner yet.

Command What it does init Detects the provider and CI system, then writes glassops.yaml and a CI file doctor Checks the config, tools, git checkout and environment variables. With --auth it also logs in to targets describe Logs in to a target, runs the org Id guard and records what the target reports plan Works out the change set between two git refs validate Runs a check-only validate of the change set. On a scratch org it first seeds what a destructive change needs gate Evaluates the policy rules for a target into a signed PERMIT permit verify Checks that a PERMIT is signed, unexpired and bound to this target, commit, plan and config deploy Deploys the change set, only under a valid PERMIT, then moves the deployed tag verify After a deploy, checks that the target holds what the plan says report Summarises every result as markdown and SARIF env create, env delete, env sweep Create, delete and sweep ephemeral scratch orgs that later steps use test Runs Apex tests with coverage on a target and writes JUnit XML check Runs your own project scripts analyze Runs the Code Analyzer and records violation counts. Needs analyze.enabled: true and the glassops-analyzer image run Runs a named pipeline from glassops.yaml, such as the default pr and deploy

Commands exit 0 on pass, 1 on a failed check and 2 on a tool error, and every command except report writes a result file to .glassops/results/. See the CLI reference, the configuration reference, PERMIT and rules, Run a pipeline and the GitHub deploy guide.

docs.title: Who This Is For
docs.text:
Teams that:

  • Already use (or want to use) GitHub Actions
  • Care about auditability and compliance
  • Prefer transparent systems over black boxes

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
The image to use is ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:v1, which follows the latest 1.x release. For a reproducible run, use ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:1.0.0 or pin the image by digest. To build from a checkout instead, run go build -o glassops ./cmd/glassops for the CLI or docker build -t glassops . for the container image.

On GitHub, examples/consumer/ is the smallest working layout. It holds a glassops.yaml and two short workflows that call the reusable workflows glassops-pr.yml and glassops-deploy.yml from this repository. The deploy caller passes GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY by name, and the value lives only as a secret of the protected glassops-deploy environment. See the GitHub deploy guide. Or run glassops init in a Salesforce DX project to generate a similar setup.

docs.title: The GlassOps Protocol
docs.text: GlassOps is governance-first. We prioritize architectural health and "One Trigger Per Object" discipline over raw deployment speed.

docs.title: Direction
docs.text: The project is being rebuilt as a CI-agnostic command line tool. Open an issue before starting a large change so it can be checked against that direction.

docs.title: Pull Request Process
docs.text:
1. Fork the repo and create your branch from main.
  2. Clean Room Standard: Ensure your contribution is independent of any proprietary or work-related logic.
  3. Test: Run go test ./... at the repository root.
  4. Lint: Ensure the CI build passes and follow the project's Go coding standards.
  5. Issue: Submit your Pull Request!

docs.title: Report Bugs
docs.text:
We use GitHub issues to track public bugs. Report a bug by opening a new issue.

Great Bug Reports tend to have:

  • A quick summary and background.
  • Specific steps to reproduce (including sample code).
  • Expected vs. actual outcomes.
  • Notes on troubleshooting steps you’ve already attempted.

docs.text: This page describes how the released glassops CLI is put together. Everything here is in v1.1.0. For the commands and flags, see the CLI reference.

docs.title: 1. The idea
docs.text:
GlassOps is one command line tool that runs inside your CI. The CI holds the secrets and starts the run. GlassOps works out what changed, checks it, decides whether it may be deployed, deploys it, and then checks that the target holds what was planned.

The decision is a file. glassops gate writes a signed PERMIT, and glassops deploy refuses to touch a target without a valid one for exactly this change.

graph LR
    Plan[plan] --> Validate[validate]
    Validate --> Gate[gate]
    Gate -->|allow| Deploy[deploy]
    Gate -->|deny| Stop[run stops]
    Deploy --> Verify[verify]
    Verify --> Report[report]

docs.title: 2. Components
docs.text: Part What it does CI system Holds secrets, starts the run and supplies the commit, the pull request and the approvals. GitHub Actions, Bitbucket Pipelines and GitLab CI are supported. The last two have not run on a real runner yet glassops CLI One Go binary, also shipped as a container image. Each step is its own command, and glassops run runs a named pipeline of them Provider The part that talks to the deploy target. Salesforce is built in. Provider exec runs your own commands for any other deploy tool. See the exec provider Config glassops.yaml names the targets, their tiers, the policy rules and the pipelines. See the configuration reference Result files Every step writes one JSON result to .glassops/results/. Later steps and report read them PERMIT The signed decision in .glassops/permit.json. See PERMIT and rules

docs.title: 3. The deploy pipeline
docs.text:
The default deploy pipeline runs six steps against one target.

  1. plan works out the change set between two git refs. With no --from, it starts from the git tag glassops/deployed/<target>, which marks the last commit deployed to that target. With no tag yet, the whole source is planned.
  2. validate runs a check-only validation of the change set against the target. It never deploys. It records which plan it validated.
  3. gate evaluates the policy rules over the plan, the CI context and the earlier results, then writes a signed PERMIT. A deny is written and signed too, and the run stops.
  4. deploy verifies the PERMIT first, then checks that the working tree is the PERMIT's commit with no modified tracked files, then logs in and deploys. When the PERMIT holds a passed validation of this plan, it quick deploys that validation. It then moves the deployed tag.
  5. verify reads the target back and checks that it holds what the plan says.
  6. report summarises every result as markdown and SARIF. It also runs after a failed step.

The default pr pipeline runs the checks without a deploy. See Run a pipeline.

docs.title: 4. The PERMIT
docs.text:
A PERMIT records one decision: whether one plan may be deployed to one target. It binds to the target, the commit, the plan, the change set and the config. Change any of them after gate ran and the PERMIT no longer matches.

  • Rules. gate runs seven built-in rules: plan_not_empty, window.<tier>, blackout, coverage_min, destructive_needs_label, separation_of_duties and analyzer_max_severity. Every rule runs, so a deny lists every reason.
  • Fail closed. Missing evidence is never a pass. A tool problem while gathering evidence denies.
  • Signing. By default the PERMIT is signed with HMAC-SHA256 using GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY. On GitHub Actions it can be signed keyless with Sigstore instead. See Sigstore signing.
  • Your own rules. Optional Rego rules run after the built-in rules. They can add denials and can never turn a deny into an allow.

docs.title: Secrets stay in CI
docs.text: The deploy target never holds deployment secrets. CI holds them and passes them to GlassOps as environment variables. glassops.yaml only names the variables, so no secret value goes in the file.

docs.title: The signing key stays out of pull request jobs
docs.text: Anyone who can run a job with GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY can sign an allow. Keep the key in a protected CI environment that only the deploy job uses. glassops doctor warns when the key is set on a pull request run. Sigstore signing removes the shared key.

docs.title: The org Id guard
docs.text: Before any step does anything to a target, the guard compares the org the login reached with the target in the config. A mismatch stops the command. Tier prod needs a production org and tier ephemeral needs a scratch org.

docs.title: Isolated logins
docs.text: Every command that talks to a Salesforce org runs the Salesforce CLI with its own temporary home directory. It never reads or writes the logins on the machine, and the directory is removed when the command ends.

docs.title: What is never logged
docs.text: Results, annotations and error messages never contain tokens, private keys, auth URLs, the org's company name or full usernames.

docs.title: 6. Results and evidence
docs.text:
• Every command exits 0 on pass, 1 on a failed check and 2 on a tool error.
  • Every step writes .glassops/results/<step>.json in one envelope, described by schemas/result.json.
  • gate writes the facts it evaluated to .glassops/facts.json.
  • report writes a markdown summary and SARIF.
  • Opt-in extras are a pull request comment and OpenTelemetry export. See PR comment and OpenTelemetry.

docs.title: 7. Failure modes
docs.text: Failure Behaviour Recovery Policy denies gate exits 1 with a signed deny. deploy never starts Fix the change, or meet the rule, and run again Evidence cannot be gathered gate denies and exits 2 Fix the tool or network problem and run again PERMIT does not match deploy exits 2 before any login Run gate again for the current commit and plan Login reaches the wrong org The guard exits 2 Fix the target Id or the credentials CI is down No deploy runs Deploy by hand with your deploy tool, outside GlassOps

docs.title: 8. Repository layout
docs.text:
• cmd/glassops: the CLI entry point.
  • internal/cli: one file per command.
  • internal/core: config, policy, PERMIT, guard, pipeline, report and telemetry.
  • internal/providers: the Salesforce and exec providers.
  • internal/ci: the GitHub, Bitbucket, GitLab and local CI layers.
  • schemas: the JSON schemas for the config and the result files.
  • examples: working layouts for each CI system.

docs.title: Deploy with GitHub
docs.text:
This guide sets up pull request checks and a deploy to production on GitHub. Two reusable workflows in this repository run the glassops container image for you. Your repository calls them with a few lines each. examples/consumer/ is the smallest working layout, and glassops init writes a similar glassops.yaml and workflow into your project. For what a PERMIT is, see PERMIT and rules.

Reusable workflow Runs Triggered by glassops-pr.yml glassops run pr pull_request glassops-deploy.yml glassops run deploy, in a protected environment a push to main

The pipelines are the ones in your glassops.yaml. See Run a pipeline for the defaults.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A glassops.yaml with a Dev Hub target and a target named prod with tier prod, each with a login. See the configuration reference and Authentication.
  • A GitHub environment named glassops-deploy. Give it required reviewers if you want an approval before the deploy job runs, and a deployment branch rule that allows main only. The run's approval is read as evidence for the separation of duties rule.
  • The variables in the table below.
  • A Salesforce connected app that allows the JWT bearer flow, for the logins. Salesforce describes it in Authorize an org using the JWT bearer flow. You get the consumer key (SF_CLIENT_ID) from the connected app, and you keep the private key that matches its certificate (SF_JWT_KEY).
Variable Used by Where it lives SF_JWT_KEY The JWT login of every target: the private key, as PEM text Repository secret SF_CLIENT_ID The JWT login of every target: the connected app's consumer key Repository secret SF_USERNAME The Dev Hub target's login Repository secret SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID The Dev Hub target's id, which the guard checks the login against Repository secret SF_PROD_USERNAME The prod target's login Repository secret SF_PROD_ORG_ID The prod target's id, checked by the guard Repository secret GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY gate signs the PERMIT with it, deploy verifies it. Make one with openssl rand -base64 48. It must decode to at least 32 bytes Secret of the glassops-deploy environment, never of the repository

The names are the ones in the glassops.yaml that glassops init writes. If your auth and id fields name other variables, use those names instead.

The key must never be available to pull request jobs. Anyone who can run a job with the key can sign an allow PERMIT. A secret held only in the glassops-deploy environment reaches only jobs that name that environment, and you control which branches may use it. glassops doctor warns when GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY is set on a pull_request or pull_request_target run.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
Save this as .github/workflows/pr.yml:

name: glassops pr

on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  glassops:
    uses: glassops-platform/glassops/.github/workflows/glassops-pr.yml@v1
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write
      security-events: write
    with:
      targets: devhub
    secrets:
      SF_JWT_KEY: ${{ secrets.SF_JWT_KEY }}
      SF_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_CLIENT_ID }}
      SF_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.SF_USERNAME }}
      SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID }}
      SF_PROD_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.SF_PROD_USERNAME }}
      SF_PROD_ORG_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_PROD_ORG_ID }}

Permissions. The calling job must grant pull-requests: write, because the workflow grants it to its job so that glassops report can post the pull request comment. A called workflow cannot hold more than its caller grants, so a caller that grants less is refused when the run starts. A pull request from a fork gets a read-only token whatever the caller grants, so there the comment warns and is not posted, and the run is not affected.

The workflow checks out full history, runs glassops run pr, uploads the SARIF file to code scanning, and keeps the results as an artifact. It never receives the permit key.

Input Default Meaning image ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:v1 The container image. Pass the glassops-analyzer image when analyze.enabled is true targets Space separated target names to log in to before the pipeline, so a bad login fails early upload-sarif true Upload the SARIF file. Needs code scanning on the repository

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Save this as .github/workflows/deploy.yml:

name: glassops deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  glassops:
    uses: glassops-platform/glassops/.github/workflows/glassops-deploy.yml@v1
    permissions:
      contents: write
      actions: read
      issues: read
      pull-requests: read
      id-token: write
    with:
      environment: glassops-deploy
    secrets:
      GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY: ${{ secrets.GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY }}
      SF_JWT_KEY: ${{ secrets.SF_JWT_KEY }}
      SF_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_CLIENT_ID }}
      SF_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.SF_USERNAME }}
      SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID }}
      SF_PROD_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.SF_PROD_USERNAME }}
      SF_PROD_ORG_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_PROD_ORG_ID }}

glassops-deploy.yml takes the inputs image, environment (default glassops-deploy) and targets, like the pull request workflow.

The permit key is passed by name. The caller must list GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY under secrets, because a called workflow does not see environment secrets unless the caller passes them. The workflow declares the secret required: true, so a caller that omits it fails. The value lives only as a secret of the protected glassops-deploy environment. Do not add it as a repository secret. The deploy job runs in that environment, so the reviewers and branch rules you set there apply to it.

Permissions. The calling job needs these, because a called workflow cannot hold more than its caller grants:

Permission Why contents: write The runner pushes the glassops/deployed/prod tag actions: read gate reads this run's environment approvals pull-requests: read gate reads the pull request behind the commit, its author and labels issues: read gate reads who added an approval label id-token: write Sigstore keyless signing of the PERMIT, when policy.permit.signing is sigstore. The reusable workflow grants it to its job, so the caller must grant it too or GitHub refuses to start the run. HMAC signing does not use it

docs.title: What the deploy job does
docs.text:
1. Checks out full history. A shallow clone is an error, never an empty plan.
  2. Installs a glassops command on the runner that runs the image with docker run --rm, one container per command, with the workspace mounted at /work. The checkout, the tag push and the uploads run on the runner, not in the container.
  3. Logs in to each target in targets, when set, with glassops doctor --auth --target <name>.
  4. Runs glassops run deploy. With the default pipeline that is plan --target prod, validate --target prod, gate --target prod, deploy --target prod, verify --target prod and report.
  5. Pushes the deployed tag. deploy moves the git tag glassops/deployed/prod inside the container, but the container has no git credentials, so its own push is only a warning. A runner step after the container exits pushes the glassops/deployed/* tags with the checkout's credentials. Without that tag, the next plan has no record of this deploy and starts from the merge base instead.
  6. Runs glassops report (also after a failure), and uploads .glassops/results/, plan.json and permit.json as the glassops-deploy-evidence artifact.

One deploy runs at a time per environment. A queued deploy waits and is never cancelled.

docs.title: How the steps fit together
docs.text:
• Plan. With --target prod and no --from, plan starts from the glassops/deployed/prod tag. If that tag does not exist yet, this is the first deploy and the whole source is planned.
  • Validate. A check-only validate against prod. It records which plan it validated, so gate can bind it into the PERMIT.
  • Gate. Evaluates the rules and writes .glassops/permit.json. A deny exits 1, so the run stops here and the deploy never starts.
  • Deploy. Verifies the PERMIT, then logs in and deploys. When the PERMIT holds a passed validation of this plan, it quick deploys it.
  • Report. Runs after a failed step, writes the run summary and SARIF, and exits with the worst status of the results.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The references say @v1. @v1 follows the latest 1.x release, and the :v1 image tag moves with it. For a reproducible run, pin a release tag such as @v1.0.0 or a commit SHA, and set the image input to a version tag such as 1.0.0 or to an image digest.
  • Separation of duties needs the rule in glassops.yaml. When the person who merges is also the pull request author, the rule fails unless an approval satisfies it. Set approval.environment: glassops-deploy so an approval of the environment satisfies the rule. See PERMIT and rules.
  • The container runs as root, so files it writes under .glassops/ are owned by root on the runner.
  • The warning about the tag push inside the container appears on every deploy. That is expected, because the runner step pushes the tag.

docs.title: Other CI systems and single commands
docs.text:
glassops is one binary, so any CI can run glassops run pr and glassops run deploy with the same glassops.yaml. On GitHub, the glassops-platform/glassops action runs one command in the container, for steps that do not fit a pipeline:

- uses: glassops-platform/glassops@v1
  with:
    command: doctor --auth --target prod
    env: |
      SF_JWT_KEY
      SF_CLIENT_ID
  env:
    SF_JWT_KEY: ${{ secrets.SF_JWT_KEY }}
    SF_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_CLIENT_ID }}

docs.title: Run GlassOps on Bitbucket or GitLab
docs.text:
GlassOps runs the same pipelines on GitHub Actions, Bitbucket Pipelines, GitLab CI and a laptop. The CLI picks the CI from the environment it runs in (GitHub first, then Bitbucket, then GitLab), or from the global flag --ci github|bitbucket|gitlab|local.

Not proven on a real runner. The Bitbucket and GitLab layers are written from Atlassian's and GitLab's documentation of their predefined variables, and they are covered by unit tests that set those variables. No pipeline has run on a real Bitbucket or GitLab runner yet. Every statement on this page about a real runner is untested. Treat your first run as the proof.

Working files are in the repository: examples/bitbucket and examples/gitlab. Or run glassops init in the project. It writes bitbucket-pipelines.yml or .gitlab-ci.yml when it detects that CI.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Salesforce DX project with a glassops.yaml, or run glassops init in it.
  • A signing key for the PERMIT, stored only where the deploy job can read it. Make one with openssl rand -base64 48.
  • The login secrets that glassops.yaml names with $VAR.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Both examples run the container image ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:v1, which holds the CLI, the Salesforce CLI and sfdx-git-delta. See Releases, images and licenses for the tags and for how to build the image yourself.

docs.title: What the CI layer does
docs.text:
A CI layer tells GlassOps who is running what, and gives it somewhere to put outputs and a summary.

Bitbucket Pipelines GitLab CI Detected from BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER is set GITLAB_CI is true Repository BITBUCKET_REPO_FULL_NAME CI_PROJECT_PATH Commit BITBUCKET_COMMIT CI_COMMIT_SHA Actor UUID of whoever started the build (BITBUCKET_STEP_TRIGGERER_UUID) GITLAB_USER_LOGIN Run Id BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER CI_PIPELINE_ID Pull request BITBUCKET_PR_ID is set CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE is merge_request_event Event name pull_request for a pull request, push for everything else pull_request for a merge request, push when the source is empty, any other source passed through as it is Base branch BITBUCKET_PR_DESTINATION_BRANCH CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME

Bitbucket exposes no user name, so the actor is a UUID. GitLab's user email variable is never read.

docs.title: Outputs and the summary
docs.text:
Neither CI has a command channel like GitHub's GITHUB_OUTPUT, so GlassOps writes files and you publish them as artifacts:

  • Step outputs (status and result) are appended as NAME=value lines to .glassops/outputs.env. A name must be letters, digits and underscores, and a value must be one line.
  • The run summary is appended as markdown to .glassops/summary.md.
  • Set GLASSOPS_OUTPUT_FILE or GLASSOPS_SUMMARY_FILE to move either file. A relative path is relative to the project directory.

On GitLab, .glassops/outputs.env is a dotenv file, so the job can publish it with artifacts:reports:dotenv and later jobs read the values as variables. Annotations are plain log lines, such as error: ....

docs.title: What is not read
docs.text: Approval evidence (the PR author, labels and environment approvals) is not read from Bitbucket or GitLab. The separation of duties rule needs that evidence, so on these CIs it can be enforce or off per tier but it cannot decide on an approval. See PERMIT and rules.

docs.title: Usage on Bitbucket
docs.text:
1. Enable Pipelines for the repository.
  2. Add the variables glassops.yaml names with $VAR (for example SF_JWT_KEY) as secured repository variables.
  3. Create a production deployment environment, restrict it to main, and add GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY as a secured variable of that environment only. Make the value with openssl rand -base64 48. The pull request pipeline never sees it.
  4. Copy bitbucket-pipelines.yml to the repository root.

The file clones with depth: full so change sets between commits are complete, runs glassops run pr on pull requests, and runs glassops run deploy on a push to main in the production deployment. Both save .glassops/** as artifacts.

docs.title: Usage on GitLab
docs.text:
1. Add the variables glassops.yaml names with $VAR as masked CI/CD variables.
  2. Protect the default branch. Add GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY as a CI/CD variable that is protected, masked and limited to the production environment. The merge request pipeline never sees it.
  3. Copy .gitlab-ci.yml to the repository root.

The file sets GIT_DEPTH: "0" for the full history and entrypoint: [""] on the image, because GitLab needs a shell to run script lines.

docs.title: Moving the deployed tag
docs.text:
After a successful deploy, GlassOps moves the git tag glassops/deployed/<target> in the checkout, and tries to push it. The next plan --target starts from that tag.

  • The Bitbucket example pushes glassops/deployed/* itself after glassops run deploy.
  • On GitLab, a job token usually cannot push, so moving the tag only warns until you give the job a credential that can push. Without the push, the next plan falls back to the merge base with the target's branch.

A failed push is a warning, never a failed deploy, because the deploy has already happened.

docs.title: What you can check without a runner
docs.text: You can run the CI layer's mapping on your own machine by setting the variables by hand, for example CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE=merge_request_event GITLAB_CI=true glassops doctor, and reading the result file. That checks the mapping, not the runner. Whether a real runner sets the variables as documented, whether the artifacts are collected, and whether the dotenv report reaches later jobs are the parts that stay untested here.

docs.title: Run a pipeline
docs.text: glassops run <pipeline> runs a whole list of steps from glassops.yaml in one command. It runs the same way on a laptop and in any CI system, so a pipeline you run locally is the one your CI runs. The commands it calls are described in the CLI reference.

docs.title: Run it locally
docs.text:
From the project root, with git, the Salesforce CLI, sfdx-git-delta (sf plugins install sfdx-git-delta) and the environment variables your targets name:

glassops run pr --dry-run   # print the steps, run nothing

--dry-run shows each step, its when and the global flags it receives. It writes nothing and removes nothing. A real run writes one result file to .glassops/results/ per step, plus run.json for the whole run. The exit code is the worst of all steps: 0 pass, 1 a check or policy failed, 2 a tool error. Add .glassops/ to your .gitignore: init does not, and the directory holds generated plans, PERMITs and results.

A fresh init project does not finish glassops run pr on a laptop. The default pr pipeline is written for a pull request in CI, and two things are missing outside one:

  • plan has no base. Outside a pull request, --from auto needs a target or a base branch, so the first step stops with "--from auto needs a target or a pull request base branch. Pass --from." Every later step is skipped except those marked when: always.
  • environments.ephemeral is not configured. env create and env delete need that entry and a Dev Hub target, so env delete fails with "environments.ephemeral is not configured". See environments.

To run something that finishes, add a pipeline of your own to glassops.yaml that names the base and leaves out what you have not set up. This one plans from the previous commit, runs your project scripts and reports:

pipelines:
  local:
    - plan --from HEAD~1
    - check
    - step: report
      when: always

glassops run local

Add validate --target prod before report to run a check-only validate against a real target. That logs in to the target with the credentials in your environment. The CI pipeline is the same steps with a base the CI provides, so a local local pipeline is a rehearsal and not the CI run.

docs.title: Run it in CI
docs.text:
In any CI, run the same command in the glassops container image, or with a glassops binary on the runner:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work \
  -e SF_JWT_KEY -e SF_CLIENT_ID -e SF_USERNAME -e SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID \
  ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:<version> run pr

run is in v0.4.0 and later. See Install.

On GitHub, the reusable workflows do this for you and add the checkout, the SARIF upload and the evidence upload. See Deploy with GitHub. For a single command outside a pipeline, the glassops-platform/glassops action takes command: run pr or any other command line.

docs.title: The default pipelines
docs.text:
A project with no glassops.yaml gets these two pipelines, exactly as config.DefaultPipelines() returns them. glassops init writes them into the file it creates. A glassops.yaml that has no pipelines key has none, and one that has the key uses only what it lists.

pipelines:
  pr:
    - plan
    - check
    - analyze
    - env create
    - validate --target ephemeral --fallback-target prod
    - step: report
      when: always
    - step: env delete
      when: always
  deploy:
    - plan --target prod
    - validate --target prod
    - gate --target prod
    - deploy --target prod
    - verify --target prod
    - step: report
      when: always

pr. Plans the change, runs your project scripts (check), runs the Code Analyzer (analyze), creates a short-lived scratch org named ephemeral from the Dev Hub (env create), and runs a check-only validate there. --fallback-target prod makes validate use the prod target when no environment exists, for example when environments.ephemeral is not configured. report and env delete run even after a failure, so the run always leaves a summary and never leaves an org behind. validate runs the tests at the configured test level. To run the tests with coverage minimums as a separate step, add test --target ephemeral after validate.

deploy. Plans from what prod last received (--target prod starts from the glassops/deployed/prod tag), validates, asks the policy rules for a signed PERMIT, deploys under it, and then runs verify to check that the target holds what the plan says. A denied gate exits 1 and the deploy step is skipped. report runs either way. The deploy needs GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY, which should be available only to the protected deploy job. See Deploy with GitHub.

Two steps skip themselves when they have nothing to do. check does nothing without check.scripts, and analyze does nothing without analyze.enabled: true. Both end with the status empty and exit 0.

docs.title: Write your own
docs.text:
A step is a glassops command line without the glassops prefix, or a map. Add when to decide what runs after a failure, and an exec step to run any shell command.

pipelines:
  pr:
    - plan
    - step: exec
      run: npm run build
    - env create
    - validate --target ephemeral
    - test --target ephemeral
    - step: report
      when: always
    - step: env delete
      when: always
when The step runs success (the default) Only when no earlier step failed failure Only when an earlier step failed always Every time, including after a failure or a cancel

How run treats the steps:

  • Empty plan. After plan writes an empty plan, every later step that is not when: always is skipped. A pull request that changes no deployable source passes without logging in anywhere. A plan that cannot be read is an error, never an empty plan.
  • Failure. A step fails when its exit code is not 0. Later success steps are skipped. failure and always steps still run. The run exits with the worst code.
  • Exec steps. An exec step runs sh -c in the project directory. It gets GLASSOPS_RESULTS_DIR, the absolute path of the results directory, so a script can read or add to the results. Any non-zero exit is a fail. A command that cannot start is an error. The result is exec.<n>.json, with n counting exec steps from 1.
  • Same flags everywhere. Every glassops step receives the run's --dir, --config, --results-dir and --ci.
  • Stale results. A real run first removes run.json and the glassops result files left in the results directory by an earlier run, and keeps everything else. A report step cannot read an old run as evidence for this one.
  • Cancel. Ctrl+C or SIGTERM stops the current step, skips the rest, and still runs the when: always steps. The run exits at least 2.

A created environment is used automatically by later steps. env create writes .glassops/env/ephemeral/env.json and a login file, and validate --target ephemeral finds them. See env create.

docs.title: Scratch org definitions and settings
docs.text: glassops env create makes a Salesforce scratch org for a pull request from a definition file. It reads the same file sf org create scratch reads, including the settings block, and applies the settings before it reports the org ready. This page says what is applied, what is refused, and what happens when the org refuses a setting.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Dev Hub target in glassops.yaml and an environments entry that names it.
  • A scratch org definition file in the project.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Nothing extra. env create uses the Salesforce CLI in the GlassOps image.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Point the environment at the file with definition:

environments:
  ephemeral:
    devhub: devhub
    definition: config/project-scratch-def.json
    ttl_days: 1

docs.title: What the definition may hold
docs.text:
Key Handled as edition, features, hasSampleData, language, country, description, release, sourceOrg Fields of the scratch org request. A list becomes a semicolon list orgName Ignored on purpose. The org is named after the environment so that env delete and env sweep can find it settings Converted to Settings metadata and deployed to the new org. See below Any other key Refused. env create names the keys it cannot apply and creates no org

env create reads and converts the whole definition before it asks the Dev Hub for an org. A definition it cannot apply never creates an org, so you do not pay an org to find out.

docs.title: How settings are applied
docs.text:
Each key under settings that ends in Settings becomes one file. For example lightningExperienceSettings becomes LightningExperience.settings-meta.xml. The files go into a throwaway source project and deploy to the new org with sf project deploy start --test-level NoTestRun, after the login to the new org works. Fields keep the order the definition gives them. A list becomes one element per item, and a nested object becomes a nested element.

The conversion refuses, with a message that names the field:

  • objectSettings, because it describes object metadata and not a Settings type.
  • A key that does not name a Settings type, such as one that does not end in Settings.
  • A settings block that is not an object.
  • A field name that is not a valid element name.
  • A null value, or a list inside a list.
  • The same key twice in one object.

docs.title: When the org refuses a setting
docs.text:
Some settings need features the edition or the Dev Hub does not have. The org then fails the settings deploy. What env create does:

  1. It deletes the new scratch org, even when the run itself was stopped.
  2. It records a failed create check that lists each failure as <type> <name>: <problem>, followed by "The scratch org was deleted", and exits 1. env.json records the attempt.
  3. If the delete also fails, the check is an error, the command exits 2 and the message says "Deleting the scratch org failed too" with the reason. env.json is written, so env delete or env sweep can remove the org later.

Exit 1 means the definition is at fault and no org is left. Exit 2 means the tooling failed: the deploy never got an answer, the result could not be read, or an org may still exist. The run never goes on in an org that is missing part of what its definition asked for.

The result records salesforce.settings (the member names), salesforce.settings_deployed, salesforce.settings_deploy_id when the org reported one, and salesforce.settings_org_deleted after a failure.

docs.title: What was tested
docs.text: The conversion and the refusal path are covered by unit tests with a fake sf. How a real org answers depends on its edition and features, and some settings are refused there. A setting can also come back different from what the definition set. Run your own definition once and retrieve the settings you depend on before you trust them in a pull request pipeline.

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: glassops is one Go binary that runs each delivery step as its own command. The goal is a governed pipeline that runs the same way in any CI system or on a laptop. Salesforce is the first provider.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command What it does glassops init Detects the provider and the CI system, then writes glassops.yaml and a CI file glassops doctor Checks the config, the tools, the git checkout and the environment variables the config names. With --auth it also logs in to targets glassops describe Logs in to one target, runs the guard, and records what the target reports about itself glassops plan Works out what changed between two git refs and writes the manifests and a change set glassops validate Runs a check-only validate of the change set against a target glassops gate Evaluates the policy rules for a target and writes a signed PERMIT glassops permit verify Checks that a PERMIT is signed, unexpired and bound to this target, commit, plan and config glassops deploy Deploys the change set to a target, only under a valid PERMIT glassops verify After a deploy, checks that the target holds what the plan says glassops report Summarises every result for the CI and writes SARIF glassops env create Creates the ephemeral environment (a scratch org) that later steps use glassops env delete Deletes that environment glassops env sweep Deletes old environments that a cancelled run left behind glassops test Runs Apex tests with coverage on a target and writes JUnit XML glassops run Runs a whole pipeline from glassops.yaml glassops check Runs your own project scripts glassops analyze Runs the Code Analyzer and records the violation counts

docs.title: glassops init
docs.text:
• Detects a Salesforce project from sfdx-project.json.
  • Detects the CI system from the project files (.github, bitbucket-pipelines.yml, .gitlab-ci.yml, azure-pipelines.yml) or from the environment it runs in.
  • Writes glassops.yaml with commented stub targets and the default pr and deploy pipelines.
  • For GitHub, also writes .github/workflows/glassops.yml, which runs glassops doctor on full git history. Other CI systems are detected but get no CI file yet.
  • Never overwrites a file unless you pass --force.
  • Does not touch .gitignore. Add .glassops/ to it yourself. That directory holds the plan, the PERMIT, the results and the deployed-tag bookkeeping, and none of it belongs in git. Run git status after your first command to see it appear.

docs.title: glassops doctor
docs.text:
Runs these checks and fails if any of them fails:

  • glassops.yaml, when present, against the schema and its rules. Without the file, the defaults are used.
  • The provider: the config and the project files must agree.
  • The tools: git always, plus sf and the sfdx-git-delta plugin for Salesforce projects. Versions are recorded.
  • The analyzer, only when analyze.enabled is true: Java 11 or newer and the Code Analyzer plugin (tool.java and tool.code-analyzer). Both are in the glassops-analyzer image.
  • Opt-in features, only when you turn them on: cosign and the signing identity, issuer and repository for Sigstore signing, and opa and the policy files for Rego rules.
  • The checkout: a shallow clone fails, because it would make every change set empty. On GitHub, use actions/checkout with fetch-depth: 0.
  • The environment: every $VAR the config names must be set. Only presence is checked. Values are never printed or stored.
  • The PERMIT key: on a pull_request or pull_request_target run, GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY should not be set. If it is, doctor adds a permit.key check whose detail starts with warning: and a CI warning annotation. This never fails the command. Only presence is checked. See PERMIT and rules.

docs.title: glassops doctor --auth
docs.text:
Adds a login to each target in the config, or only the one named by --target, and runs the guard on it. Without --auth, doctor never logs in. The environment check covers every $VAR the config names. With --auth --target, it covers only that target's variables, so a target that does not exist yet, such as a scratch org that a later step creates, does not fail the check.

Flag Meaning --auth Also log in to targets and run the guard --target With --auth, check only this target

docs.title: glassops describe
docs.text:
Logs in to one target, runs the guard, and writes what the target reports about itself to .glassops/results/describe.json. A guard mismatch exits 2 before anything else runs.

Flag Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required)

docs.title: glassops plan
docs.text:
Works out the change set between two git refs. It writes the provider's manifests to .glassops/plan/ and the change set to .glassops/plan.json. For Salesforce, sfdx-git-delta works out the delta and the project's .forceignore applies. A shallow clone is an error, never an empty plan. For Salesforce, plan also reads the checked out source of each changed Apex class and records the classes annotated @IsTest in the fact salesforce.apex_test_classes, and the classes whose top level type is an interface or enum, which have no executable lines and no coverage, in the fact salesforce.apex_nonexecutable_types. The check looks at the annotations before the first class keyword, after it strips comments and strings. It is not an Apex parser, and a class it cannot read is treated as a normal class. With a full scope, plan lists the whole source instead, and it reads no git history. See the plan scope below.

Flag Default Meaning --from auto Base git ref, or auto --to auto Head git ref, or auto (HEAD) --target Target the plan is for, used by --from auto and the plan scope. A name under targets or environments --scope full or delta. Overrides the config for this run

With --from auto, a pull request uses the merge base with its base branch. With --target, auto uses the git tag glassops/deployed/<target>, then the merge base with the target's branch. Without either, pass --from.

On a laptop, outside a pull request, there is no base: --from auto without --target stops with "--from auto needs a target or a pull request base branch. Pass --from." For a first run, name the base yourself:

glassops plan --from HEAD~1

First deploy rule: with --target and --from auto, a target that has no glassops/deployed/<target> tag has never received a deploy from glassops. plan then plans the whole source instead of a delta, prints a notice, and records the facts plan.first_deploy and plan.from_source: first-deploy. A shallow clone is still an error.

Plan scope: full plans the whole source and delta plans what changed. plan takes the first of these that is set: --scope, then targets.<target>.plan.scope for the --target given, then salesforce.delta.enabled, then delta. A full scope never looks up a tag or a merge base, so a shallow clone does not matter. A delta scope still follows the first deploy rule. Use scope: full on a scratch org target, where a delta would fail on components the empty org does not have, and keep production on delta. plan records the facts plan.scope and plan.scope_source, and doctor prints the scope every target gets.

docs.title: glassops validate
docs.text:
Logs in to the target, runs the guard, and runs a check-only validate of the change set in .glassops/plan.json. It never deploys. See Validate is check-only.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --fallback-target Target to use when --target is not configured or not reachable --plan <dir>/.glassops/plan.json Change set file --check-only true Always true. false is refused

A target counts as not configured when it is missing from glassops.yaml or when its id variable is not set, for example because the scratch org was never created. A guard mismatch never falls back. The test level comes from salesforce.test_level for the tier of the target used, then its default entry, then the Salesforce CLI's own default. An empty change set ends with status empty and no login. When the Salesforce CLI stops watching a validate that is still running, for example because its wait ran out, validate waits on sf project deploy report until the org gives the final status, so a validate still in progress is never read as a failure. validate records the facts validate.plan_sha256, validate.change_set_sha256 (the hash a PERMIT binds the change set by) and validate.test_level, which gate uses to decide whether a deploy may reuse the validation. See validation binding.

docs.title: glassops gate
docs.text:
Reads the change set, the earlier results in the results directory and the CI context. It builds the facts for one target, runs the policy rules over them, and writes a signed PERMIT to .glassops/permit.json. It writes the PERMIT whether the answer is allow or deny, and it deletes any PERMIT already at that path first, so an old allow never survives a failed run. Unless --no-connect is set, it logs in to the target and runs the guard. The rules, the PERMIT and the evidence gate reads are described in PERMIT and rules.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --plan <dir>/.glassops/plan.json Change set file --permit <dir>/.glassops/permit.json Where the PERMIT is written --no-connect false Do not log in. The PERMIT records the configured Id and the kind the guard requires for the tier, and the guard check is skipped --deploy-command Provider exec only. The command deploy -- will run, as a JSON array of strings, such as '["./deploy.sh","--prod"]'. The PERMIT binds its SHA-256, never the text. With any other provider it is an error

When the target's tier has deploy windows and the gate's clock is inside one, the PERMIT expires when that window closes, if that is before policy.permit_ttl. Windows that overlap or touch extend it. With no window for the tier, or a clock outside them, the PERMIT keeps the full TTL, and the window rule decides.

A blackout shortens the PERMIT too. When a blackout that covers the target's tier has not ended by today (UTC), the PERMIT expires when it begins, at 00:00 UTC on its first day, if that is before the TTL and before any window end. A PERMIT issued before a blackout can never be valid inside it. An ephemeral target is not checked against blackouts, so its PERMIT is not shortened. deploy needs no separate blackout check, because the config is bound by hash and the expiry is checked at deploy.

Needs GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY, unless policy.permit.signing is sigstore. Then it needs a GitHub Actions job with id-token: write and cosign instead, see Sigstore signing. With policy.rego set it also runs your Rego rules with opa. Reads .glassops/plan.json, .glassops/results/plan.json and .glassops/results/validate.json when they exist, and the CI context. Writes .glassops/permit.json, .glassops/facts.json and .glassops/results/gate.json.

Exit When 0 The PERMIT allows the deploy 1 Policy denies the deploy. The signed PERMIT is still written 2 GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY is missing or unusable, the plan file is missing or unreadable, the target is not in the config, or evidence could not be gathered. A missing key, plan or target writes no PERMIT. Evidence that could not be gathered writes a signed PERMIT that denies

Result facts: gate.allow, gate.ephemeral, gate.permit_id, gate.expires_at, gate.expires_at_window_end (true when the window end set the expiry), gate.expires_at_blackout_start (true when a blackout start set the expiry), and gate.deploy_command_sha256 when --deploy-command was given.

docs.title: glassops permit verify
docs.text:
Checks a PERMIT without logging in to the target, so any deploy tool can honour it. It checks the key, the signature, that the PERMIT allows, that it has not expired, that its lifetime is sound, and that it matches the target, the commit, the plan, the change set and the config. The order is in PERMIT and rules.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --permit <dir>/.glassops/permit.json PERMIT file --plan <dir>/.glassops/plan.json Change set file --deploy-command Provider exec only. The command deploy -- is about to run, as the same JSON array of strings gate --deploy-command takes. The PERMIT must bind exactly this command. With any other provider it is an error

Without --deploy-command the command is not checked, as deploy without -- does not check it. With it, a PERMIT that binds no command, or another one, fails (exit 1).

Needs GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY, unless policy.permit.signing is sigstore. Then it needs cosign and a pinned repository instead, see Sigstore signing. Reads the PERMIT, the change set, the plan files under .glassops/plan/, glassops.yaml and the CI commit. Writes .glassops/results/permit-verify.json.

Exit When 0 The PERMIT holds 1 The PERMIT does not hold: bad signature, denied, expired, a different target, commit, plan, config, change set or deploy command, a file that is not a readable PERMIT, or plan files changed after plan 2 The key is missing or unusable, or the PERMIT file, the change set, the config or the commit cannot be read or found, or --deploy-command is not a JSON array of at least one string or is used with a provider other than exec

Result facts: permit.key_id, permit.id and permit.expires_at.

docs.title: glassops deploy
docs.text:
Verifies the PERMIT before it logs in. Then it runs the guard and deploys the change set in .glassops/plan.json. When the PERMIT holds a validated deploy Id, it quick deploys that validation. See validation binding. Success is read from the target's result body. After a successful deploy it moves the git tag glassops/deployed/<target> to the deployed commit and pushes it. The tag is lightweight. A failed move or push is a warning, because the deploy has already happened: the tag check is skipped, deploy.tag_pushed is false, and the CI gets a warning annotation. A checkout with no remote called origin gets that warning too, never a failure. A target of tier ephemeral keeps no tag, because its org does not outlive the run. deploy then moves and pushes nothing, the tag check is skipped with no warning, and deploy.tag_pushed is false.

The local tag stays. The tag is moved in your checkout before the push, so it stays there when the push fails. A rerun of plan --target <target> then starts from the deployed commit and finds nothing to deploy. If the push did not happen and you want the plan to start from the old base again, delete the local tag:

git tag -d glassops/deployed/prod

A deploy the target reports as failed lists one problem line per component failure, per test failure and, when the status is not Succeeded, per coverage warning.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --plan <dir>/.glassops/plan.json Change set file --permit <dir>/.glassops/permit.json PERMIT file --wait the provider's How long to wait for the deploy, such as 30m. The Salesforce provider waits 60 minutes --resume Job Id of an earlier deploy to wait on again. Skips quick deploy. Accepted only when .glassops/results/deploy.json records that job timing out under the same PERMIT and target

With provider exec, a command after -- runs instead of exec.deploy: glassops deploy --target prod -- ./ci/deploy.sh. See the exec provider. A command after -- with any other provider is an error.

Needs GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY and a git checkout. The deployed commit is the CI's commit, or git rev-parse HEAD when the CI reports none. It must be the commit the PERMIT names. After the PERMIT verifies and before the login, git rev-parse HEAD must also be that commit and no tracked file may be modified or staged. Untracked files are allowed. With provider exec, a command after -- runs only when the PERMIT binds exactly that command, from gate --deploy-command. An empty change set under a valid PERMIT ends with status empty and no login.

Exit When 0 The deploy succeeded, or the change set was empty 1 The deploy ran and the target reported failures, or salesforce.deploy.quick is require and the PERMIT holds no passed validation to quick deploy 2 The PERMIT is missing, unreadable, denied, expired or does not match, the plan files changed, the working tree is not the PERMIT's commit or git cannot tell, --resume names a job the last deploy did not time out on, login or the guard failed, or the deploy did not finish within --wait. A timeout keeps the job Id and prints the --resume command, and does not move the tag

Result facts: deploy.permit_id, deploy.plan_sha256, deploy.test_level, deploy.quick_mode, deploy.id, deploy.quick, deploy.timed_out, deploy.commit, deploy.tag and deploy.tag_pushed, plus the provider's own facts. deploy.plan_sha256 is the plan the deploy sent. deploy.test_level is the level the deploy was sent with, or for a quick deploy the level of the validation it reused.

docs.title: glassops verify
docs.text:
Runs after deploy and checks that the target holds what the plan says. It never deploys. It is the last step of the default deploy pipeline, before report.

Before it logs in, verify reads the deploy result and the change set. It stops with an error when the deploy result is for another target or provider, did not pass, did not finish (a timeout), or has no deploy Id, because there is no finished deploy to check. It checks that the plan files still match the plan digest. deploy always records deploy.plan_sha256 and deploy.test_level, so verify always ties the plan to the deploy: the recorded digest must equal the plan's digest, and the fact verify.plan_bound_to_deploy is true. It is false only for a deploy result deploy did not write. An empty deploy ends verify with status empty and no login. Then it logs in, runs the guard, and the provider runs these checks:

Check Passes when verify.status The target's deploy record says the deploy succeeded. A failed deploy lists the coverage warnings the report holds verify.check_only The deploy was not a check-only run, so it changed something verify.members Every component in the plan, and every destructive member, is in the deploy's component successes. Counts are recorded as facts and never compared, because the target's counts expand and vary verify.tests Apex tests ran when the test level needs them. A quick deploy and an empty test level skip this check. At RunRelevantTests, a plan with no Apex class or trigger may run no tests, and the check is skipped then verify.flows Every Flow in the plan whose source says Active runs as its latest version in the target, and when the deploy changed it, that version was modified after the deploy started. A Flow whose source says Draft is not checked verify.foreign_deploys No other deploy that is not check-only was created in the target between the deploy's start and now. Fails or warns according to the setting verify.smoke The verify.smoke command exits 0. Skipped when it is not set

Anything the provider cannot read, such as a query that fails, is an error and never a pass. A warning is a passing check whose detail starts with warning:. It adds a CI warning annotation and its name to the fact verify.warnings. The smoke command runs even when an earlier check failed, but not after the provider returned an error.

Settings verify.smoke, verify.foreign_deploys and verify.flows are in Verify, coverage and YAML settings. With provider exec, the provider runs exec.verify instead of the checks above. See the exec provider.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --plan <dir>/.glassops/plan.json Change set file --deploy-result <results-dir>/deploy.json Deploy result to verify

Reads the deploy result, the change set and the plan files. Writes .glassops/results/verify.json.

Exit When 0 Every check passed. Warnings still exit 0 1 A check failed 2 A tool error: the deploy result or the change set cannot be read or does not match, login or the guard failed, or the provider could not read the target

Result facts: verify.passed, verify.deploy_id, verify.deploy_quick, verify.commit, verify.permit_id, verify.plan_sha256, verify.plan_bound_to_deploy, verify.warnings and verify.smoke_exit_code, plus the provider's own facts.

docs.title: glassops report
docs.text:
Reads every result in the results directory. It writes a markdown summary to the CI's run summary, and with --summary also to a file. It writes SARIF to --sarif for policy denials found in the PERMIT and for failed checks in the validate and deploy results. SARIF files already in the results directory, such as Code Analyzer's, are merged into the output. The SARIF file it writes is skipped when it reads the directory again. report writes no result file of its own.

Flag Default Meaning --sarif <dir>/.glassops/report.sarif SARIF file to write --summary Also write the markdown summary to this file --pr-comment false On a GitHub pull request run, also post the summary as one pull request comment, created the first time and updated after. report.pr_comment: true does the same. A failed post only warns. See Pull request comment

report exits with the worst status among the results: 0 when all pass, 1 when any failed, 2 when any errored. That lets a CI run it after a failed step with if: always() and still fail the job. It also exits 2 when there are no results or one cannot be read.

docs.title: glassops env create
docs.text:
Creates the ephemeral environment named under environments in glassops.yaml, from its Dev Hub target, for later steps to use. It logs in to the hub and runs the guard on it. The default pr pipeline runs it before validate.

For Salesforce it does not run sf org create scratch. It creates a ScratchOrgInfo record in the Dev Hub (a signup), polls until the record is Active for up to 15 minutes, and exchanges the record's auth code for a login. A signup refused for capacity or a transient error is retried up to three times. A signup that is still not active after 15 minutes is not retried, because it could still become active. The scratch definition file (environments.<target>.definition) supports the keys edition, features, hasSampleData, language, country, description, release and sourceOrg. Any other key, including settings, is an error, so an org is never created without something the file asks for. orgName is replaced by the environment name.

Flag Default Meaning --target ephemeral Environment name from the environments section --name <prefix>-<repo>-<pr or branch>-<run> Environment name. The prefix is environments.<target>.prefix, default glassops. Outside CI the repo is the project directory and the run is a UTC timestamp --ttl-days environments.<target>.ttl_days, else 1 Days the environment lives --shape environments.<target>.shape Source org Id for an org shape. A $VAR is read from the environment --env-file <dir>/.glassops/env/<target>/env.json Where to write env.json

How later steps use the org. env create writes env.json and a login file. env.json records the environment name, Id, expiry and the path of the login file, and holds no secret. The login file holds an sfdx-url login, is readable only by the current user, and lives in the operating system's temporary directory. When each command runs in its own container, set TMPDIR to a mount they share. A later command that resolves a target named under environments, such as validate --target ephemeral, finds env.json and logs in with that file instead of the $VAR settings. With no env.json, the target falls back to its targets entry, and --fallback-target applies if that is not configured. An env.json that records a failed create (ready: false) counts as not configured. On GitHub, env create also sets the step outputs env_id, env_file and auth_file.

env create refuses to run when env.json already exists, so run env delete first. If the create fails after the signup was requested, env.json is still written so env delete can remove the org.

Writes .glassops/results/env-create.json with the facts env.file, env.id, env.record_id, env.name, env.auth_file and env.expires_at, plus the provider's own.

Exit When 0 The environment is active 2 environments.<target> is not configured, env.json already exists, the hub login or guard failed, or the signup failed or timed out

docs.title: glassops env delete
docs.text:
Deletes the environment from its hub. It reads env.json, or finds the environment by --name. With neither, nothing is recorded to delete: the delete check is skipped and the command exits 0. Deleting an environment that is already gone passes. After a delete from env.json, it removes the login file and env.json, so later steps fall back to the config. The default pr pipeline runs it with when: always.

Flag Default Meaning --target ephemeral Environment name from the environments section --name the one env create made Delete by name instead of from env.json --env-file <dir>/.glassops/env/<target>/env.json env.json to read

Writes .glassops/results/env-delete.json. Exit 0 when the environment is deleted, already gone, or nothing is recorded. Exit 2 when the config, the hub login or env.json (for another target or hub) is wrong, or the delete fails.

docs.title: glassops env sweep
docs.text:
Deletes every environment on the hub whose name starts with <prefix>- and that is older than --max-age, and lists what it deleted. It never matches the bare prefix. Run it on a schedule to remove environments that a cancelled run left behind.

Flag Default Meaning --target ephemeral Environment name from the environments section, which supplies the hub and the prefix --max-age environments.<target>.ttl_days as a duration Delete environments older than this, such as 24h. Must be above zero

Writes .glassops/results/env-sweep.json with the facts env.prefix, env.max_age, env.deleted and env.deleted_count. Exit 0 when the sweep finished, 2 when the config, the hub login or a delete failed.

docs.title: glassops test
docs.text:
Logs in to the target, runs the guard, and runs the target's Apex tests with code coverage. It never deploys. It writes JUnit XML and checks the result against test.coverage.

Flag Default Meaning --target Target name from glassops.yaml (required) --level test.level for the target's tier, then test.level.default Test level, such as RunLocalTests --tests Comma separated tests to run, for a level that names them --wait the provider's How long to wait for the run, such as 30m --resume Run Id of an earlier run to wait on again, instead of starting a new one --junit <results-dir>/test.junit.xml JUnit XML file to write

Coverage. Percentages are rounded down, so a rounded-up value never passes a minimum. Both settings are optional:

  • test.coverage.org_min compares against the org-wide coverage that sf reports. That figure counts every class in the org, so it catches classes that no test touches.
  • test.coverage.class_min compares each class that the test run reports. test sees per-class coverage only for the classes in that report, so a class that no test ran against can be missing from it. Set org_min as well to catch those.

If a minimum is set and its figure is not reported, that is a failure, never a pass. A run that does not finish within --wait fails and names the run Id, and --resume waits on it again.

No tests found. When sf reports that no Apex tests were found, test records the fact test.none_found. It fails when org_min or class_min is set, because coverage cannot be checked. When neither is set, the status is empty, the tests check is skipped, and it exits 0.

Writes .glassops/results/test.json and the JUnit file (listed as an artifact). Facts: test.ran, test.failed, test.finished, test.run_id, test.org_coverage (a whole percent, absent when unknown), test.coverage.<Class>.percent and target.source.

Exit When 0 The tests passed and every set minimum is met, or no tests were found and no minimum is set 1 A test failed, the run did not finish, coverage is below a minimum or was not reported, or no tests ran while a minimum is set 2 The target could not be resolved, the login or guard failed, or the tests could not be run

docs.title: glassops run
docs.text:
Runs the steps of one pipeline from glassops.yaml, in order, in one process. See Run a pipeline for the default pipelines.

glassops run pr
glassops run deploy --dry-run
Flag Default Meaning --dry-run false Print the steps and the global flags each one gets. Runs nothing and removes nothing

A step is a glassops command line such as validate --target prod, or a map with step, when and, for an exec step, run.

When a step runs. when decides what happens after an earlier step failed.

when The step runs success (the default) Only when no earlier step failed failure Only when an earlier step failed always Every time, including after a failure or a cancel

A step has failed when its exit code is not 0. After a plan step that exits 0, run reads .glassops/plan.json. An empty plan skips every later step that is not when: always, with the reason "the plan is empty". A plan that cannot be read is an error (exit 2), and later success steps are skipped, so it is never read as an empty plan. A cancel (Ctrl+C or SIGTERM) stops the current step and skips the rest except when: always steps, which still run with up to 2 minutes each. A cancelled run exits at least 2.

Exec steps. A step named exec runs its run command with sh -c in the project directory. The command inherits the environment and gets GLASSOPS_RESULTS_DIR, the absolute path of the results directory. Its output goes straight to the run's output. A zero exit passes and any other exit is a fail (exit 1). A command that cannot start, is stopped by a signal or is cancelled is an error (exit 2). Each exec step writes exec.<n>.json, where n counts exec steps from 1, with one command check and the facts exec.run, exec.index and exec.exit_code.

Global flags. Every glassops step receives this run's --dir, --config, --results-dir and --ci, so all steps read one project and write to one results directory.

Stale results. Before the first step, a real run removes run.json and every top-level *.json file in the results directory whose schema is glassops.result/v1. It does not recurse and keeps every other file, such as SARIF and JUnit files. This stops an earlier run from reading as evidence for this one. The count is the fact run.stale_removed. A removal failure exits 2 before any step runs.

Exit code. The worst exit code of all steps. Any code other than 0 and 1 ranks as 2.

Writes .glassops/results/run.json with the facts run.pipeline, run.steps (index, step, when, argv, result, exit code, duration, skip reason), run.exit_code, run.empty_plan, run.cancelled and run.stale_removed, and one check per step. A pipeline that is not in the config, or a step that does not parse, exits 2 before anything runs.

With telemetry.otlp.endpoint set, run sends the finished run to an OpenTelemetry collector as trace spans after it writes the record. A failed export only warns. See OpenTelemetry export.

docs.title: glassops check
docs.text:
Runs your own project scripts, such as lint or unit test commands, and records the outcome. It does not replace those tools.

Scripts come from check.scripts in glassops.yaml, a list of name and run entries. Each runs with sh -c in the project directory, in order, and every script runs even after an earlier one failed. A script's output goes to the log and never into the result.

Flag Default Meaning --script Run only the script with this name. An unknown name is an error

Writes .glassops/results/check.json with one check per script named script.<name> and the facts check.scripts, check.passed and check.failed. With no scripts configured the status is empty and the exit code is 0.

Exit When 0 Every script exited 0, or none are configured 1 A script exited non-zero 2 sh could not start, or --script names no entry

docs.title: glassops analyze
docs.text:
Runs the Salesforce Code Analyzer over the project and records how many violations it found. It runs only when analyze.enabled: true is set in glassops.yaml. Without that, it records a skipped check, the status empty, and exits 0.

The analyzer needs Java 11 or newer and the Code Analyzer plugin of the Salesforce CLI. The standard glassops image has neither, so run analyze in the separate glassops-analyzer image, which adds them. glassops doctor checks for Java and the plugin when analyze.enabled is true. Only the Salesforce provider is supported.

Flag Default Meaning --rule-selector analyze.rule_selector, else Recommended Rules to run --sarif <results-dir>/analyze.sarif SARIF file to write

analyze does not decide what is too severe. It exits 0 whatever it found, so long as the analyzer ran. The gate rule analyzer_max_severity reads the counts and decides. It writes .glassops/results/analyze.json with the facts analyze.rule_selector, analyze.total and analyze.sev1 to analyze.sev5. The SARIF file and the analyzer's own JSON (.glassops/analyze/code-analyzer.json, beside the results directory) are listed as artifacts, and report merges the SARIF file into its output.

Exit When 0 The analyzer ran, or analyze is off 2 The analyzer could not run, its output could not be read, or the provider is not Salesforce

docs.title: The smart seed
docs.text:
A destructive change, such as a deleted field, cannot be validated on a fresh scratch org, because the component it deletes was never there. When validate runs against a scratch org and the change set has destructive members, it first deploys the base state they need. The base ref is the plan's from ref. salesforce.ephemeral.seed chooses how:

Mode What it deploys minimal (the default) Only the destructive members, from the base ref, plus the parent object of any child component (field, record type, validation rule and similar) whose parent is a custom object (__c, __mdt or __e) full The whole source at the base ref off Nothing. The destructive change is validated against the org as it is

If a minimal seed fails because something else is missing (an error such as Entity 'Widget__c' not found), the seed falls back to the full seed, records validate.seed.fallback: true and raises a CI warning. A failed seed stops validate before it runs. The seed applies to scratch targets only. validate records validate.seed.mode, validate.seed.fallback and validate.seed.members.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Each target names its login under auth. There are three methods, and every secret value is a $VAR that names an environment variable. Values stay in your CI's secret store and never go in the file.

Method Fields Notes jwt username, client_id, key, optional instance_url key is a $VAR that holds the private key as PEM text. A value that is not PEM text is read as the path of a key file sfdx-url url url is a $VAR that holds a force:// auth URL access-token token, instance_url token is a $VAR that holds an access token 
targets:
  devhub:
    id: $SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID
    tier: devhub
    auth: { method: jwt, username: $SF_USERNAME, client_id: $SF_CLIENT_ID, key: $SF_JWT_KEY }
  ephemeral:
    id: $SF_EPHEMERAL_ORG_ID
    tier: ephemeral
    auth: { method: sfdx-url, url: $SF_EPHEMERAL_AUTH_URL }

docs.title: Isolated Salesforce CLI state
docs.text: Every command that talks to an org runs the Salesforce CLI with its own temporary home directory (HOME and USERPROFILE). It never reads or writes the Salesforce CLI logins you have on your machine. The temporary directory, and any key file written into it, is removed when the command ends, including when it is stopped with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. Logins are retried only on network and server errors, never on a bad key, an unknown user or an expired token.

docs.title: The guard
docs.text:
Before any step does anything to a target, the guard compares the org the login reached with the target in the config. A mismatch exits 2.

  • The Id is compared on its first 15 characters, case-sensitively, so a 15 and an 18 character form of one Id match.
  • A target with no Id configured fails, because it cannot be checked.
  • Tier prod and tier devhub need a production org.
  • Tier ephemeral needs a scratch org.
  • Every other tier checks the Id only.

docs.title: What is never logged
docs.text: Results, step outputs, CI annotations and error messages never contain the org's company name, tokens, private keys, auth URLs or full usernames. Usernames are masked to their first character and domain, such as u***@example.com. Email-shaped text in a tool's error message is masked the same way.

docs.title: Validate is check-only
docs.text: validate is check-only by construction. It only ever runs sf project deploy validate, never a deploy, and --check-only=false is refused. After the run it reads the full result with sf project deploy report and exits 2 if the target reports anything other than a check-only run. Keep a Dev Hub for managing scratch orgs, and validate against a scratch org or a sandbox.

docs.title: Global flags
docs.text: Flag Default Meaning --dir . Project root --config <dir>/glassops.yaml Config file --results-dir <dir>/.glassops/results Where results are written --ci auto CI system: auto, github, bitbucket, gitlab or local. See Bitbucket and GitLab

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Pass 1 A policy or check failed. The tool itself worked 2 A tool or infrastructure error stopped the command, or the command line was invalid

A tool error is printed to stderr as glassops: <message> on one line. A line break inside the message is replaced, so output that a CI runner scans for commands cannot start a new line.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Every command writes .glassops/results/<step>.json in one envelope, described by schemas/result.json:

{
  "schema": "glassops.result/v1",
  "step": "doctor",
  "status": "pass",
  "started": "2026-10-26T12:00:00Z",
  "ended": "2026-10-26T12:00:02Z",
  "provider": "salesforce",
  "checks": [{ "name": "tool.sf", "status": "pass", "detail": "2.155.7" }],
  "facts": { "tools.sf": "2.155.7" },
  "artifacts": [],
  "errors": []
}

status is one of pass, fail, error, skipped or empty.

On GitHub, each command also sets the step outputs status and result (the result file path), adds an error annotation for each failed check, and writes a table to the job summary.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: glassops.yaml is optional. Every key, with an example, is in the configuration reference. The schema is schemas/config.json.

docs.title: End-to-end check
docs.text: The workflow cli-e2e.yml creates a scratch org in a Dev Hub, runs doctor --auth, plan and validate against it, and deletes the org. It runs on demand and on pushes to main, and it skips with a notice when the Salesforce secrets are not set. The scripts are in scripts/e2e.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The current release is v1.0.0 on the releases page. Releases, images and licenses says which release first has each command and feature.

Route What you get What you need Published image ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:v1, or 1.0.0 for a fixed release The release binary with Node 22, the Salesforce CLI and sfdx-git-delta Docker go build -o glassops ./cmd/glassops The current binary Go 1.27.4 or later, and the host tools below docker build -t glassops . The current binary in an image with the tools, plus cosign and opa Docker. Add docker build -f Dockerfile.analyzer -t glassops-analyzer . for analyze

A built Linux binary also runs inside the published image. Mount it over the image's own:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work -v "$PWD/glassops:/usr/local/bin/glassops"   ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:1.0.0 doctor

Host prerequisites for go build. git always. For a Salesforce project also the Salesforce CLI sf and its sfdx-git-delta plugin:

sf plugins install sfdx-git-delta

Provider exec needs only git and sh. ./glassops doctor checks the tools and says which one is missing. Release tags, image tags, the license scan and the third party notices are described in Releases, images and licenses.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
glassops.yaml is optional. Without it, the commands use their defaults and the default pipelines. The schema is schemas/config.json. It rejects keys it does not know, so a typo is an error. glassops doctor validates the file.

Secrets are never written in the file. A secret field names an environment variable with a $VAR value, and the value stays in your CI's secret store.

Beyond the schema, these rules are checked:

  • Org Ids look like Salesforce org Ids, unless written as a $VAR.
  • No two targets share an org Id.
  • At most one target has tier prod.
  • Every policy window names a time zone that exists, and its from and to differ.
  • Every blackout has valid dates and ends on or after its start date.
  • policy.permit_ttl is a duration from 5 minutes to 24 hours.
  • A separation of duties approval sets environment or label, and a label needs approvers.
  • Every environments.<name>.devhub names a configured target.
  • No pipeline step is empty.
  • With provider exec, exec.paths lists at least one path.
  • With policy.permit.signing: sigstore, both identity and issuer are set, and repository (when set) is owner/name.
  • Every telemetry.otlp.headers value is a whole $VAR reference.
  • The file stays inside the YAML limits: an alias that refers to itself is refused, and so are files nested deeper than 64 levels or expanding past 100000 values.

Names (targets, tiers, environments, pipelines) are lowercase letters, digits, _ and -, starting with a letter.

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text: Key Required What it holds version yes The schema version. Always 1 provider no salesforce or exec. Detected from the project files when absent, except exec, which is never detected targets no Orgs that changes go to, with their login policy no Deploy windows, blackouts and the rules gate evaluates salesforce no Salesforce provider settings environments no Ephemeral environments that env create makes test no Test levels and coverage minimums for test check no Project scripts that check runs analyze no Code Analyzer settings verify no Settings for verify. See Verify, coverage and YAML settings exec no The commands provider exec runs. See The exec provider telemetry no Opt-in export of run spans to an OpenTelemetry collector. See Pull request comment and OpenTelemetry export report no Settings for report. See Pull request comment and OpenTelemetry export pipelines no Named lists of steps for run

docs.title: version and provider
docs.text:
version: 1
