provider: salesforce

docs.title: targets
docs.text:
One entry per org. The key is the target name that --target takes.

Field Meaning id What the login must land on (the guard), or a $VAR holding it. For Salesforce it is an org Id, 15 or 18 characters. For provider exec it is a plain Id that your exec.describe prints: letters, digits and . _ : / -, starting with a letter or digit, compared exactly tier A name that policy windows, rules and test levels key on. prod, devhub and ephemeral have fixed meaning in the guard branch The git branch that deploys to this target. plan --from auto uses its merge base when the target has no deployed tag auth The login. See Authentication plan.scope full or delta, for plan --target with this target. It wins over salesforce.delta.enabled. See plan scope

A name under environments can also have an entry here, to set its tier or plan.scope. Its org Id and login still come from env create.

targets:
  ephemeral:
    plan: { scope: full }
  devhub:
    id: $SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID
    tier: devhub
    auth: { method: jwt, username: $SF_USERNAME, client_id: $SF_CLIENT_ID, key: $SF_JWT_KEY }
  prod:
    id: $SF_PROD_ORG_ID
    tier: prod
    branch: main
    auth: { method: jwt, username: $SF_PROD_USERNAME, client_id: $SF_CLIENT_ID, key: $SF_JWT_KEY }

docs.title: policy
docs.text:
What gate evaluates. The rules are described in PERMIT and rules.

Field Meaning windows Per tier, a list of allowed deploy windows: days, from, to (24 hour HH:MM) and tz (an IANA zone) blackouts Date ranges (from, to, optional tiers and reason) when no deploy is allowed rules coverage_min, analyzer_max_severity, separation_of_duties, destructive_needs_label permit_ttl How long a PERMIT stays valid, from 5m to 24h. The default is 2h permit How PERMITs are signed: signing (hmac, the default, or sigstore), and for sigstore the identity, issuer and repository. See Sigstore signing rego files, a list of Rego policy files that gate runs after the built-in rules. See Rego rules actors Accepted by the schema. No command reads it yet 
policy:
  permit_ttl: 2h
  windows:
    prod: [{ days: [tue, thu], from: "18:00", to: "22:00", tz: America/Chicago }]
  blackouts:
    - { from: "2026-12-20", to: "2027-01-03", tiers: [prod], reason: holiday freeze }
  rules:
    coverage_min: 75
    analyzer_max_severity: 2
    destructive_needs_label: { label: destructive-ok, tiers: [prod] }
    separation_of_duties:
      tiers: [prod]
      approval: { environment: glassops-deploy }

docs.title: salesforce
environments
docs.text:
One entry per ephemeral environment, keyed by the target name the environment registers as. The default pr pipeline uses the name ephemeral. See env create.

Field Meaning devhub The target that creates the environment (required) definition Scratch definition file, relative to the project root ttl_days Days the environment lives. The default is 1 shape Source org Id for an org shape, or a $VAR holding one prefix Starts every environment name. The default is glassops 
environments:
  ephemeral:
    devhub: devhub
    definition: config/project-scratch-def.json
    ttl_days: 1

docs.title: test
docs.text:
Settings for glassops test.

Field Meaning level Map of tier to test level, with a default key. The --level flag overrides it coverage.org_min Minimum org-wide coverage, 0 to 100 coverage.class_min Minimum coverage for each class the test run reports, 0 to 100 coverage.class_scope Which classes no test touched count at 0%: changed (the default) or all. See Verify, coverage and YAML settings 
test:
  level: { default: RunLocalTests }
  coverage: { org_min: 75, class_min: 75 }

docs.title: check
docs.text:
Scripts that glassops check runs with sh -c.

check:
  scripts:
    - { name: lint, run: npm run lint }
    - { name: unit, run: npm test }

docs.title: analyze
docs.text:
Settings for glassops analyze. Nothing runs until enabled is true.

Field Meaning enabled true turns analyze on. It also needs the glassops-analyzer image rule_selector Code Analyzer rules to run. The default is Recommended max_severity The default for policy.rules.analyzer_max_severity, 1 (critical) to 5. The policy value wins when both are set 
analyze:
  enabled: true
  rule_selector: Recommended
  max_severity: 2

docs.title: pipelines
docs.text:
Named lists of steps for glassops run. Each step is a string (a glassops command line without the glassops prefix) or a map with step, optional when (success, failure or always) and, for the step exec, a run shell command. A pipeline needs at least one step.

pipelines:
  pr:
    - plan
    - check
    - step: exec
      run: npm run build
    - step: report
      when: always

The default pr and deploy pipelines apply only when the project has no glassops.yaml. A file that has a pipelines key replaces them, and one without the key has no pipelines, so glassops run pr fails with an unknown pipeline. glassops init writes the defaults into the file. See Run a pipeline.

docs.title: The exec provider
docs.text:
The exec provider lets any deploy tool run under GlassOps. GlassOps keeps the gate, the signed PERMIT, the org Id guard and the evidence. Your own commands do the validate, the deploy and the verify. Use it when the target is not Salesforce, or when you deploy with a tool that GlassOps has no built-in provider for.

The provider is never detected from the project files, and glassops init does not write an exec project. You write glassops.yaml yourself. A minimal project has four small scripts. This one was run end to end in the GlassOps image with a built binary: doctor --auth, plan, validate, gate, deploy, verify all passed.

glassops.yaml:

version: 1
provider: exec
exec:
  paths: [app]
  describe: ./ci/describe.sh
  validate: ./ci/validate.sh
  deploy: ./ci/deploy.sh
  verify: ./ci/verify.sh
targets:
  prod:
    id: prod-eu-1
    tier: prod
    branch: main
pipelines:
  deploy:
    - plan --target prod
    - validate --target prod
    - gate --target prod
    - deploy --target prod
    - verify --target prod
    - step: report
      when: always

An exec project has no default pipelines, because init never detects exec. Without a pipelines: block glassops run deploy fails with an unknown pipeline. The block above is the same steps the Salesforce default deploy pipeline runs.

The target id is a plain Id that your exec.describe prints. It may hold letters, digits and . _ : / -, and must start with a letter or digit. It is compared exactly, and two targets may not share one. A Salesforce project still needs an org Id or a $VAR there.

ci/describe.sh reports the target. kind is production for tier prod:

#!/bin/sh
echo '{"id": "prod-eu-1", "kind": "production"}'

ci/validate.sh and ci/verify.sh can be as small as exit 0 while you start. Replace them with real checks.

ci/deploy.sh does the deploy and writes an engine result. The id in that result is what verify needs. Without it the deploy result has no deploy.id, and verify stops with exit 2 because there is no finished deploy to check.

#!/bin/sh
set -eu
echo "deploying to $GLASSOPS_TARGET"
# ... run your deploy tool here ...
cat > "$GLASSOPS_RESULTS_DIR/exec-deploy.json" <<JSON
{"schema": "glassops.engine-result/v1", "step": "deploy", "passed": true, "id": "release-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)", "components_deployed": 1}
JSON

Make the scripts executable with chmod +x ci/*.sh, and add .glassops/ to .gitignore.

docs.title: Run it step by step
docs.text:
GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY is needed from gate on, and not before. Make one and set it in the shell, or as an environment secret in your CI. plan and validate do not read it.

export GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 48)"

glassops doctor --auth --target prod
glassops plan --from HEAD~1 --target prod
glassops validate --target prod
glassops gate --target prod --deploy-command '["./ci/deploy.sh"]'
glassops deploy --target prod -- ./ci/deploy.sh
glassops verify --target prod
glassops report

The gate and deploy lines bind and run an explicit command, as Deploying explains. Leave out --deploy-command and -- ./ci/deploy.sh to run exec.deploy from the config instead. glassops run deploy runs the same steps from the pipeline, with exec.deploy. The first plan --target prod for a target with no deployed tag plans every file under exec.paths.

In PowerShell the JSON needs quoting that depends on the version. In PowerShell 7.3 and later, single quotes are enough:

glassops gate --target prod --deploy-command '["./ci/deploy.sh"]'

In Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell before 7.3, the double quotes inside are dropped on the way to the program, and gate refuses the value as not a JSON array. Escape them with a backslash:

glassops gate --target prod --deploy-command '[\"./ci/deploy.sh\"]'

Both forms were run on PowerShell 7.6 and 5.1 against a built binary. The scripts above are shell scripts, so on Windows they run from Git Bash or WSL.

glassops doctor checks that sh and git exist. It does not check your commands.

docs.title: The exec section
docs.text:
Every command is a shell command that runs with sh -c in the project directory. Only paths is required.

Key What it is exec.paths Project paths whose changed files make up the plan. Required, at least one. Each is relative to the project root. An absolute path, a path that climbs out with .. and a path that starts with : are refused exec.plan Optional. Runs after GlassOps writes its own plan files and may add more files to $GLASSOPS_PLAN_DIR. A non-zero exit fails plan exec.describe Prints {"id": "...", "kind": "..."} for the target. See The guard exec.validate The check-only run. Required to run validate exec.deploy The deploy. Required to run deploy, unless you pass a command after -- exec.verify The post-deploy check. Required to run verify

A step whose command is not set is an error, never a pass. A step that ran nothing must not look like one that succeeded.

docs.title: What plan does
docs.text:
plan lists the files under exec.paths that changed between the two refs, using git diff for a delta and git ls-tree for a full plan. It writes two files into .glassops/plan/:

  • changes.txt lists the files added or modified. It is the manifest.
  • deleted.txt lists the files deleted. It exists only when something was deleted, and it is the destructive manifest.

Each file has one path per line, relative to the project root, with forward slashes, sorted. A file name that holds a newline cannot be listed and is refused. The plan digest covers everything in .glassops/plan/, including files exec.plan adds. The PERMIT binds that digest and the commit, so it binds both the file list and the file content. A plan with no changed files and no extra files is empty.

docs.title: What every command gets
docs.text:
Each command runs with your process environment plus these variables:

Variable Value GLASSOPS_RESULTS_DIR Absolute path of the results directory GLASSOPS_TARGET Target name, when the step has a target GLASSOPS_TARGET_ID Target Id, when the step has a target GLASSOPS_PLAN_DIR Absolute path of the plan directory GLASSOPS_PLAN Absolute path of .glassops/plan.json, when it exists GLASSOPS_PERMIT Absolute path of .glassops/permit.json, when it exists GLASSOPS_FROM, GLASSOPS_TO The plan's git refs. exec.plan only GLASSOPS_DEPLOY_ID The deploy Id from the deploy result. exec.verify only

GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY is removed from every command's environment. A deploy tool that could read the signing key could sign its own PERMIT. GlassOps verifies the PERMIT before it runs your deploy command, so the command does not need the key.

Your own credentials stay in the environment, because the exec provider logs in to nothing itself. Put them in the CI's secret store and pass them to the job.

docs.title: The result file
docs.text:
A command may write <results-dir>/exec-<step>.json to say more than its exit code can. The step is plan, validate, deploy or verify. The shape is schemas/engine-result.json:

{
  "schema": "glassops.engine-result/v1",
  "step": "deploy",
  "passed": true,
  "id": "release-2026-11-08",
  "components_deployed": 12,
  "problems": [],
  "facts": { "exec.region": "eu-1" }
}
Field Rule schema Must be glassops.engine-result/v1 step Must match the step that ran passed Required id Optional for plan, validate and deploy, but needed for verify. The run's Id, such as a deploy Id. deploy records it as deploy.id, and verify stops with exit 2 when deploy.json has none components_deployed Optional. A count of zero or more problems Optional. One line per failure facts Optional. Every key must start with exec.

The file may hold no other field and no second JSON value. GlassOps deletes an earlier result file before each command, so an old file can never stand in for the current run.

How the outcome is decided:

  • With no result file, the exit code decides. Zero passes.
  • A pass needs exit code zero and passed: true.
  • Exit zero with passed: false fails.
  • A non-zero exit with passed: true fails, and the problem says so.
  • A result file that does not match the schema is an error, not a failure.

docs.title: The guard
docs.text:
The guard compares the org Id the target reports with the Id in the config. The exec provider has no login, so exec.describe is how a target reports itself. It prints one JSON object on stdout:

{"id": "prod-eu-1", "kind": "production"}

kind is one of production, sandbox, scratch or unknown. The Id is compared exactly. Tier prod and devhub need kind: production, and tier ephemeral needs scratch.

  • A target of tier prod must have exec.describe. Without it every command that reaches the guard stops with an error, because nothing may touch production without the check.
  • Any other tier may leave exec.describe out. The guard is then recorded as skipped with the reason, and the configured Id is used as it is.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
glassops deploy --target prod verifies the PERMIT, runs the guard, then runs exec.deploy. The exec provider has no quick deploy and cannot resume. --resume is refused. Run the deploy again instead.

You can name the command on the command line and leave exec.deploy out, but the PERMIT must bind it. Give gate the same command as a JSON array of strings, one element per argument:

glassops gate --target prod --deploy-command '["./ci/deploy.sh","--region","eu-1"]'
glassops deploy --target prod -- ./ci/deploy.sh --region eu-1

gate stores only the SHA-256 of the array in the PERMIT, as deploy_command_sha256, and never the text. Everything after -- replaces exec.deploy for that run, and each argument is passed as one word. deploy refuses any other command, and refuses a PERMIT with no command hash, with exit 2 and before it runs anything. ["a b"] and ["a","b"] hash differently. The result records exec.deploy_override: true. A command after -- with any other provider is an error, and so is --deploy-command. Without a command after --, exec.deploy runs and the PERMIT binds the config file, which holds that command.

docs.title: Verifying
docs.text: glassops verify --target prod runs exec.verify with GLASSOPS_DEPLOY_ID set. The check verify.exec passes or fails on the result above, and each problem line becomes a failing check named verify.exec.problem.N. Set exec.verify if your deploy pipeline has a verify step, as the example above does. verify also needs the deploy result to hold a deploy id, which the deploy script writes in its result file. See glassops verify.

docs.title: Untested here
docs.text: The provider is covered by unit tests with a fake shell and by the script scripts/e2e/exec-e2e.sh, which runs the binary in a container with no network. The script takes the binary's name or path as its one argument and defaults to glassops. It runs plan, gate --deploy-command, permit verify, a tampered PERMIT, a wrong describe Id, a command the PERMIT does not bind, a modified tracked file, and the deploy. No exec project has deployed to a production system through it yet.

docs.title: PERMIT and Rules
docs.text: A PERMIT is a signed file that records one decision: whether one plan may be deployed to one target. glassops gate makes the decision and writes the PERMIT. glassops deploy and glassops permit verify refuse to go on unless the PERMIT is genuine, still valid and about the thing being deployed. This page describes the PERMIT, the rules that feed it, and the evidence gate reads. The commands are in the CLI reference.

docs.title: What a PERMIT is
docs.text:
The PERMIT is JSON in .glassops/permit.json, with the schema name glassops.permit/v1. It holds:

Field Meaning id A random identifier, in hex allow true or false. A deny is recorded as a PERMIT too issued_at, expires_at When it was made and when it stops being valid. The lifetime is policy.permit_ttl, or less when the target's tier has deploy windows: the PERMIT then expires when the window that held the gate's clock closes, or when a blackout that covers the tier next begins target The target name, tier, id and kind. The Id and kind are what the login reported, unless --no-connect was used commit The commit the CI reported plan_sha256 The hash of the plan files config_sha256 The hash of glassops.yaml change_set_sha256 The hash of plan_sha256 and the change set fields that say how the plan files are used: provider, dir, manifest, the destructive list in order, empty and full deploy_command_sha256 Provider exec only, when gate ran with --deploy-command. The SHA-256 of the command as a JSON array of strings. The command text is never stored validation Optional. The deploy Id of a passed check-only validation, its test level and passed separation_of_duties How the separation of duties rule was met. See below checks Every rule result, each with its rule name, outcome and detail signature The algorithm, the key id and the signature value

A PERMIT binds to a specific target, commit, plan, change set and config. Change any of them after gate ran and the PERMIT no longer matches. A PERMIT with no change_set_sha256 was written by an older gate and is refused with a message saying so. Run gate again.

docs.title: The signing key
docs.text:
By default the PERMIT is signed with HMAC-SHA256, as described here. On GitHub Actions you can sign keyless with Sigstore instead, which needs no key. See Sigstore signing. The rest of this section is about the HMAC key.

The key comes from the environment variable GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY, which holds base64 text that decodes to at least 32 bytes with at least 8 different byte values. Standard base64 is accepted with or without padding. A shorter key, or a placeholder such as one character repeated, is refused, and the error never contains the key. One way to make a key:

openssl rand -base64 48

The key_id in the signature is the first eight hex characters of the SHA-256 of the key. It names the key without revealing it. permit verify and deploy refuse a PERMIT whose key_id differs from their own key's, with the message that it was signed with a different key.

The signature covers the whole PERMIT, with the signature value left out: keys sorted, no extra whitespace, times in UTC. The signature value must be standard padded base64, exactly as gate writes it. A PERMIT file with a field the format does not know, or with trailing data, is refused as unreadable, because such a field would not be covered by the signature.

The key must never be available to pull request jobs. Anyone who can run a job with the key can sign an allow. Put it in a protected CI environment that only the deploy job uses. glassops doctor adds a warning when GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY is set on a pull_request or pull_request_target run. See Deploy with GitHub.

docs.title: What gate does
docs.text:
gate always writes a signed PERMIT, including when policy denies the deploy. The deny is part of the record. Before it does anything else, it deletes any PERMIT already at the output path, so a stale allow can never stand in for the current run.

Two things stop it before a PERMIT is written, and both exit 2: GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY is missing or unusable, and the plan file or the target cannot be found. Everything after that still produces a signed PERMIT.

The checks in the PERMIT come in this order: the guard check, the validation.bound check, the rule results, then any evidence.* failures. The guard is the org Id and tier check described in the CLI reference. With --no-connect it does not run, the PERMIT records the configured Id and the kind the tier requires, and the guard check is skipped.

gate also writes the facts it evaluated to .glassops/facts.json.

docs.title: Fail closed
docs.text:
Missing evidence is never a pass.

  • A rule that needs a fact that is not there fails, or says so in its detail.
  • A tool or infrastructure problem while gathering evidence adds a failing evidence.<name> check. The PERMIT denies, is still signed and written, and gate exits 2 instead of 1. Examples: the guard refusing the target, a GitHub API call that fails, a result file that exists but cannot be read, a missing commit or plan hash, and plan files that no longer match the plan hash.
  • A rule set with no rules is a defect, never a pass. So is a rule source that returns no results.
  • Optional Rego rules run after the built-in rules and can only add denials. If opa or a policy file cannot be used, the PERMIT denies and gate exits 2.
  • Only the outcomes pass, skipped, waived_by_config and satisfied_by_approval allow. Any other outcome denies, including a misspelled or empty one.
  • gate owns the facts under change., ci. and target.. The change set file and earlier result files can never set them. From the earlier results in the results directory, gate reads only facts under validate., plan., analyze., test., check. and the provider's own prefix, such as salesforce.. change.destructive_count is the larger of the provider's count and the number of destructive manifests.

docs.title: The ephemeral automatic PERMIT
docs.text: A target whose login the guard accepted as a scratch org gets an automatic PERMIT. Only the org Id guard applies. The rules are not run, no GitHub API call is made, and the PERMIT carries an ephemeral check and a not_applicable separation of duties record. It is issued only when the guard really ran and saw a scratch org, so --no-connect on an ephemeral target runs the full rule set instead. The result fact gate.ephemeral says which happened.

docs.title: What permit verify and deploy check
docs.text:
Both use the same verification, in this order. The first failure is the one reported.

permit verify, before the PERMIT checks:

  1. The key. A missing or unusable key is an error (exit 2) before anything else is read.
  2. The config, the target, the change set and the commit. A problem reading any of them is an error (exit 2).
  3. The PERMIT file. A missing file is an error (exit 2). A file that is not a readable PERMIT is a failure (exit 1).
  4. The plan files. If the files under .glassops/plan/ no longer hash to the change set's plan_sha256, the plan was edited after plan and the check fails (exit 1).

deploy, before the PERMIT checks, reads the target, the change set, the config hash and the commit, then checks the plan files the same way. In deploy every refusal is exit 2, because nothing may touch the target. The login comes after verification.

The PERMIT checks, shared by both:

  1. It is signed and has a change_set_sha256.
  2. The signature: the algorithm is HMAC-SHA256, the key id matches, and the value verifies. With Sigstore signing the algorithm is sigstore-bundle and cosign checks the certificate identity, the issuer and the repository instead of a key id.
  3. The schema is glassops.permit/v1.
  4. allow is true.
  5. It has not expired.
  6. Its lifetime is sound: issued_at is set and not more than 5 minutes ahead of this clock, expires_at is after issued_at, and the lifetime is no longer than policy.permit_ttl.
  7. The target name matches.
  8. The target Id matches. Ids compare on their canonical form, so a 15 and an 18 character form of one Id are equal.
  9. The commit matches.
  10. The plan hash matches.
  11. The config hash matches.
  12. The change set hash matches.
  13. For deploy -- <command> or permit verify --deploy-command <command> with provider exec, the PERMIT binds that exact command. A PERMIT with no deploy_command_sha256, or a different one, is refused.

Checking the signature first means a forged or damaged PERMIT is rejected before any of its contents are trusted. deploy additionally compares the PERMIT against the deployed commit, which is the CI's commit, or git rev-parse HEAD when the CI reports none.

After the PERMIT verifies and before it logs in, deploy checks the working tree. git rev-parse HEAD must be the PERMIT's commit, and git status --porcelain --untracked-files=no must be empty, so no tracked file is modified or staged. Untracked files, such as .glassops itself, are not looked at. The refusal is exit 2 and names the commit and up to 10 modified paths, never file contents. When git is missing or the directory is not a repository, deploy refuses too.

deploy --resume <job> is accepted only when .glassops/results/deploy.json names that job, the same PERMIT Id and target, and records deploy.timed_out as true. Anything else is exit 2.

docs.title: Validation binding and quick deploy
docs.text:
gate can bind a check-only validation into the PERMIT, so deploy can quick deploy it instead of deploying again. It binds the validation only when all of these hold for .glassops/results/validate.json:

  • The result passed.
  • It is for the same target name.
  • It was a check-only run with a deploy Id.
  • It records the plan hash it validated (validate.plan_sha256) and that hash equals the current plan.
  • It records the change set hash it validated (validate.change_set_sha256, the same hash as the PERMIT's change_set_sha256) and that hash equals the current change set. A validate result written before this fact existed has none, so it is not bound. Run validate again.
  • It did not record that no tests ran. A validation with salesforce.tests_total 0 is not bound, because the target refuses to quick deploy it.

The PERMIT then carries validation with the deploy Id and the recorded test level. The validation.bound check says whether it was bound and why not. It never denies. Without a bound validation, deploy runs a full deploy.

How deploy uses it depends on salesforce.deploy.quick in glassops.yaml:

Value Behaviour prefer (default) Quick deploy the bound validation. If the target refuses it, fall back to a full deploy and record salesforce.quick_refused require Quick deploy only. With no passed validation in the PERMIT, deploy fails with exit 1 before any login. If the target refuses the quick deploy, no full deploy runs off Always run a full deploy

The target refuses a quick deploy when the validation was never run, was already deployed, or is more than ten days old. It also refused one in testing when another deploy reached the target after the validation, so run any other deploy to the same target after deploy, not between validate and deploy.

At RunRelevantTests, Salesforce picks the tests from the Apex in the change set. A change set with no Apex class or trigger runs no tests, so its validation is not bound and deploy runs a full deploy. Do not combine RunRelevantTests with quick: require, or every change set with no Apex fails at deploy.

docs.title: The v1 rules
docs.text:
gate runs these seven rules, in this order. Every rule runs, so the PERMIT lists every reason for a deny. Only a fail outcome denies. The outcomes are pass, fail, skipped, waived_by_config and satisfied_by_approval.

Rule Outcomes plan_not_empty fail if the plan has no changes, or the facts do not say. Otherwise pass window.<tier> See below blackout See below coverage_min See below destructive_needs_label See below separation_of_duties See below analyzer_max_severity See below

docs.title: window.<tier>
docs.text:
Named after the target's tier, such as window.prod. Configured as policy.windows.<tier>, a list of weekly windows with days, from, to and tz.

  • skipped when no window is configured for the tier.
  • pass when now is inside any window for the tier.
  • fail when now is outside every window, or a window cannot be used (an unknown time zone or a bad clock).
  • fail, under the plain name window, when the tier is unknown and any window is configured anywhere.

Times are wall clock times in the window's zone, so the window moves with daylight saving time. A window is from up to but not including to. A window whose to is earlier than its from runs past midnight and belongs to the day it starts on. A window where from equals to never matches.

docs.title: blackout
docs.text:
Configured as policy.blackouts, a list with from and to dates (YYYY-MM-DD), optional tiers and an optional reason. Dates are compared in UTC, because a blackout has no time zone, and both ends are included.

  • skipped when no blackouts are configured.
  • fail when today (UTC) falls in a blackout that covers the target's tier. An empty tiers list covers every tier. When the tier is not known, every blackout in range counts.

The rule refuses a gate that runs inside a blackout. gate also ends the PERMIT when the next blackout for the tier begins, so a PERMIT issued earlier expires before it and is refused inside it. deploy does not look at blackouts itself, because the config is bound into the PERMIT by hash and the expiry is checked at deploy. - pass otherwise.

docs.title: coverage_min
docs.text:
Configured as policy.rules.coverage_min, a whole number from 0 to 100.

  • skipped when it is not set.
  • fail when the plan facts do not list the changed Apex classes.
  • Otherwise it checks each changed Apex class against the per class coverage facts from the validate result. A class below the minimum fails. A class with no coverage fact fails too, unless it is a test class. Salesforce reports no coverage for test classes. plan reads each changed class file and records the ones annotated @IsTest (any case, with or without arguments) in the fact salesforce.apex_test_classes. Those are treated as test classes whatever their names, and the detail says how many and why. A @IsTest method inside a normal class does not make the class a test class. An Apex interface or enum has no executable lines, so Salesforce lists no coverage for it. plan also records the changed classes whose top level type is an interface or enum in the fact salesforce.apex_nonexecutable_types. Those are not measured, and the detail gives their count. An abstract class is a class and is still measured, and so is a class that implements an interface or holds an inner interface. A type in that fact that does have a coverage entry is still held to the minimum. A plan file written before these facts existed has neither, and then a name ending in Test or _Test marks a test class and an interface with no coverage fails as before.
  • pass when every class is at or above the minimum.

docs.title: destructive_needs_label
docs.text:
Configured as policy.rules.destructive_needs_label with a label and optional tiers. An empty tiers list covers every tier.

  • skipped when it is not set, or the target's tier is not covered.
  • fail when the tier is unknown, or the facts do not say how many destructive changes the plan has.
  • pass when the plan has no destructive changes.
  • With destructive changes: fail when no pull request was found, or the pull request lacks the label. pass when it has the label.

This rule has unit tests but has not yet run against a real repository.

docs.title: separation_of_duties
docs.text:
Configured as policy.rules.separation_of_duties with tiers and an optional approval. It makes sure the person who deploys is not the author of the change.

  • skipped when the rule is not set.
  • waived_by_config when the target's tier is not in tiers. An empty tiers list turns the rule off everywhere, because every tier is then outside the list.
  • Enforced when the tier is in tiers. The author is the pull request author and the deployer is the CI actor, compared without regard to case.
    • With no approval configured, it passes when both are known and differ, and fails when either is unknown or they are the same.
    • With an approval configured, it passes when they differ. When they are the same or unknown, it looks for a configured approval and gives satisfied_by_approval, or fail when none is found.

Two kinds of approval can satisfy the rule:

Mechanism Configured as Counts when environment approval.environment The run has an approved review for that environment label approval.label and approval.approvers The pull request has the label, and the person who added it is one of the approvers

A label approver may be the pull request author. The explicit approval by a listed approver is the control.

Label approval has unit tests but has not yet run against a real repository. Environment approval has run on a real project.

The PERMIT's separation_of_duties block records the result. Its mode is enforced, waived_by_config, satisfied_by_approval or not_applicable (the rule is off, or the PERMIT is an ephemeral automatic one). It also holds the author, the deployer and, for an approval, the mechanism and approver.

docs.title: analyzer_max_severity
docs.text:
Configured as policy.rules.analyzer_max_severity, a whole number from 1 to 5, where 1 is the worst.

  • skipped when it is not set.
  • skipped when there are no analyze facts, because the analyzer did not run. This is the one place a missing fact does not fail: a limit with no analysis behind it is not enforced until analysis exists.
  • fail when the facts show any violations at the configured severity or worse.
  • pass otherwise.

docs.title: Configuration example
docs.text:
version: 1
provider: salesforce
targets:
  prod:
    id: 00D000000000000
    tier: prod
    branch: main
    auth: { method: jwt, username: $SF_PROD_USERNAME, client_id: $SF_CLIENT_ID, key: $SF_JWT_KEY }
policy:
  permit_ttl: 2h
  windows:
    prod:
      - { days: [tue, thu], from: "18:00", to: "22:00", tz: America/Chicago }
  blackouts:
    - { from: "2026-12-20", to: "2027-01-03", tiers: [prod], reason: holiday freeze }
  rules:
    coverage_min: 85
    destructive_needs_label:
      label: destructive-ok
      tiers: [prod]
    separation_of_duties:
      tiers: [prod]
      approval:
        environment: glassops-deploy
    analyzer_max_severity: 2
salesforce:
  test_level:
    prod: RunLocalTests
  deploy:
    quick: prefer

permit_ttl is a duration from 5 minutes to 24 hours. The default is 2 hours.

docs.title: Evidence gate reads from GitHub
docs.text:
Some rules need facts that only GitHub knows. When the CI is GitHub and a token is available in GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN, gate reads them through the GitHub API. Without a token it reads nothing, the facts stay absent, and the rules that need them fail. The ephemeral automatic PERMIT makes no API calls. GITHUB_API_URL overrides the API address.

Read Used for Token permission GET /repos/{repo}/pulls/{number} on a pull_request run Pull request author and labels pull-requests: read GET /repos/{repo}/commits/{sha}/pulls on a push The merged pull request for the commit, its author and labels pull-requests: read GET /repos/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}/approvals Environment approvals for this run actions: read GET /repos/{repo}/issues/{number}/events Who added the approval label, only when approval.label is configured and the pull request has it issues: read

On a push, the actor is GITHUB_ACTOR, the person who pushed or merged. A push that was not merged from a pull request has no author, and a rule that needs one fails. A call that fails adds an evidence.ci.* failure, so gate denies and exits 2.

The job also needs contents: write for deploy, because it pushes the glassops/deployed/<target> tag. Without it the deploy still succeeds and only the tag push warns.

docs.title: Pull request comment and OpenTelemetry export
docs.text: Opt-in, since v1.1.0. Neither does anything until you turn it on. See what is in which release.

docs.title: Pull request comment
docs.text:
glassops report can post its summary as a comment on the pull request. It creates the comment the first time and updates the same comment on every later run, so a pull request has one GlassOps comment, not one per push.

Turn it on with the flag:

glassops report --pr-comment

or in glassops.yaml, which also covers the report step of a pipeline:

report:
  pr_comment: true

docs.title: What it posts
docs.text: The comment body is the same redacted markdown that report writes to the CI's run summary, with a hidden line <!-- glassops-report --> first. That line is how a later run finds its comment: report reads the comments on the pull request and updates the first one that holds it. A body longer than 60000 characters is cut at a line end with a note that the run summary has the rest, because GitHub rejects longer comments.

docs.title: When it applies
docs.text:
• GitHub only. On Bitbucket Pipelines and GitLab CI it posts nothing.
  • On a pull_request run only. On a push or any other event it posts nothing and adds a notice.
  • It needs the repository, the pull request number and a token. The token is GITHUB_TOKEN, or GH_TOKEN when that is not set. GITHUB_API_URL changes the API address. When something is missing, report adds a warning and posts nothing.

docs.title: Permission
docs.text:
The job needs pull-requests: write. Give it to the job that runs report and to no other. A pull request from a fork gets a read-only token, so the comment cannot be posted there. It warns instead.

The reusable workflow glassops-pr.yml grants pull-requests: write to its one job, the one that runs report. The caller must grant pull-requests: write too, because a called workflow cannot hold more than its caller grants. A caller that grants less is refused when the run starts. The workflow's other permissions stay contents: read and security-events: write.

docs.title: It never changes the result
docs.text: A comment that cannot be posted adds a warning annotation, for example "the job needs pull-requests: write", and report goes on to write the SARIF file and exits with the worst status among the results, as it always does. The comment is a convenience, so the job's result never depends on it.

docs.title: What is tested for the comment
docs.text: The calls are covered by unit tests against a local fake of the GitHub issue comments API, written from GitHub's REST documentation. The create, then update, flow has not been proven on a live pull request yet.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry export
docs.text:
glassops run can send a finished run to an OpenTelemetry collector as trace spans, so a pipeline shows up in the tracing tool you already use. It is off until you set an endpoint.

telemetry:
  otlp:
    endpoint: https://otel.example.com
    headers:
      authorization: $OTEL_AUTH_HEADER
    service_name: glassops
Field Meaning endpoint Where to send spans, over OTLP with the JSON encoding on HTTP. Setting it turns export on. A URL with no path gets /v1/traces added headers Headers to send, such as a token. Each value must be a whole $VAR reference, never the value itself. A header whose variable is not set is an error service_name The service.name in the spans. The default is glassops

No SDK is involved. GlassOps posts the JSON itself.

docs.title: What is sent
docs.text:
One run is one trace. There is a root span named glassops run, and one child span per step named glassops <step>, such as glassops gate. A span whose command exited 1 or 2 has the error status.

Only these attributes are ever sent:

Span Attributes Root glassops.duration_ms, glassops.pipeline, glassops.provider, glassops.exit_code, glassops.empty_plan, glassops.cancelled Step glassops.step, glassops.step.index, glassops.step.when, glassops.duration_ms, glassops.step.skipped, glassops.step.outcome (pass, fail, error or skipped), glassops.exit_code when the step ran, and glassops.target.name and glassops.target.tier when the step names a target that is in your config

The resource carries service.name and nothing else. Fact values, logins, org Ids, error text and command output are never copied into a span. Target names and tiers are sent, so do not put anything private in a target name.

docs.title: Safety rules
docs.text:
• Headers are sent only over https. Plain http is accepted for a loopback host such as localhost, so you can test against a local collector. Headers over plain http to any other host are refused.
  • The endpoint must not hold credentials. Use headers.
  • An export waits up to 10 seconds.
  • A failed export adds a warning annotation, for example run: telemetry export failed. It never changes the exit code, and it runs after the run record is written.
  • Every $VAR in headers is covered by the glassops doctor environment check, like the variables of a target.

docs.title: What is tested for the export
docs.text: The output was sent to otel/opentelemetry-collector 0.140.0 with an OTLP HTTP receiver and a file exporter, after a three step pipeline whose second step failed. The collector accepted it without a warning and wrote one trace with the spans described above. No export has been sent from a CI job to a hosted tracing service.

docs.title: Rego rules
docs.text:
Opt-in, since v1.1.0. Without policy.rego in glassops.yaml, gate runs only its built-in rules. See what is in which release.

The built-in rules in PERMIT and rules cover the common cases. When you need a rule of your own, gate can run Rego policies after them. A Rego rule can only add a denial. It can never turn a failed built-in rule into a pass.

GlassOps does not evaluate Rego itself. It runs the separate program opa, which is in both GlassOps images (see Releases, images and licenses). A working example with tests is in examples/rego.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
List the Rego files in glassops.yaml. Relative paths are resolved against the project directory.

policy:
  rego:
    files: [policy/deploy.rego]

gate then runs this for the target it checks, after the built-in rules:

opa eval --format json --input <facts file> --data policy/deploy.rego data.glassops.deny

An ephemeral target gets the automatic PERMIT and its rules are not run, so Rego is not run for it either.

docs.title: What your policy sees
docs.text:
The input is the facts document that gate builds and also writes to .glassops/facts.json:

{
  "schema": "glassops.facts/v1",
  "facts": { "target.tier": "prod", "salesforce.profiles": ["Admin"] }
}

These are the same facts the built-in rules read, such as target.tier, ci.event, ci.actor, ci.labels, change.destructive_count and the component lists the provider records, such as salesforce.apex_classes, salesforce.permission_sets and salesforce.profiles. Run gate once and read .glassops/facts.json to see what your project produces.

The facts come from gate alone. A result file or a change set file cannot add a ci., target. or change. fact, so a policy can trust them.

docs.title: Write a rule
docs.text:
Declare package glassops and add entries to the deny set. Each entry is an object with a rule name and a detail text.

package glassops

import rego.v1

deny contains {"rule": "protected_profile", "detail": "the plan changes the Admin profile"} if {
    input.facts["target.tier"] == "prod"
    "Admin" in input.facts["salesforce.profiles"]
}

Each entry becomes a failed check named rego.<rule> in the PERMIT, and any entry denies the deploy. gate exits 1 for a denial. When the set is empty, the PERMIT gets one passing check named rego, whose detail names the files and the first 12 characters of a SHA-256 over their names and contents. That records which policy was in force.

A rule name starts with a letter or digit and holds only letters, digits, _, . and -, up to 100 characters. A detail is cut at 500 bytes, and email addresses in it are masked.

docs.title: It fails closed
docs.text:
Rego never fails open. When policy.rego is set and any of these happens, gate still signs and writes a PERMIT, the PERMIT denies, and gate exits 2:

  • opa is not on PATH.
  • A file is missing or cannot be read.
  • opa reports an error or runs longer than 2 minutes.
  • data.glassops.deny is undefined or is not a set. A file with the wrong package name leaves it undefined, so it fails instead of passing quietly.
  • An entry has no valid rule.

docs.title: Check it before gate
docs.text:
glassops doctor checks, when policy.rego is set, that opa is installed (tool.opa) and that the files load and define data.glassops.deny as a set (policy.rego).

To try your rules over made-up facts, run opa yourself. Name the files, because passing a whole folder also loads the sample inputs as data:

opa test examples/rego/deploy.rego examples/rego/deploy_test.rego
opa eval --format json --input examples/rego/facts-deny.json --data examples/rego/deploy.rego data.glassops.deny
opa eval --format json --input examples/rego/facts-pass.json --data examples/rego/deploy.rego data.glassops.deny

docs.title: Tested here, and not
docs.text:
• The evaluator is covered by unit tests with a fake opa. The example policy and its tests also run against a real opa 1.22.0, the version in the images, in a test that runs when opa is on PATH.
  • A full gate run in a workflow on GitHub has not been proven yet.

docs.title: Releases, images and licenses
docs.text: This page describes how a GlassOps release is cut, which image tags exist, and how the license scan and the third party notices work.

docs.title: What is in which release
docs.text:
v1.0.0 is the first final release, v1.0.1 is a patch release and v1.1.0 is the first minor release. The earlier tags v0.3.0, v0.4.0, v1.0.0-rc.1, v1.0.0-rc.2, v1.0.0-rc.3 and v1.1.0-rc.1 are prereleases, listed on the releases page. This table says which tag first has each command or feature, so you can tell what an older pinned version lacks. Everything in it is in v1.1.0.

docs.title: Release tags
docs.text:
A release starts when a tag such as v1.2.3 is pushed. The release workflow only starts for tags that begin like v1.2.3. scripts/release/tags.sh accepts vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with an optional suffix such as -rc1, and exits 2 for anything else, such as v1.2.3.4, so the plan job fails and nothing is published. It decides what a tag publishes, and scripts/release/test-tags.sh tests those rules.

Tag Kind Image tags GitHub release Git tag moved v1.2.3-rc1 prerelease 1.2.3-rc1, v1.2.3-rc1 marked as a prerelease none v0.4.0 prerelease, because the major version is 0 0.4.0, v0.4.0 marked as a prerelease none v1.2.3 final 1.2.3, v1.2.3, v1, latest a draft you publish yourself v1 moves to the release commit

Details:

  • The binaries go to a draft GitHub release. Publishing it stays a deliberate step.
  • The images ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops and ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops-analyzer are built for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.
  • The moving tags v1 and latest change only on a final release, so a prerelease never becomes what @v1 runs.
  • The v1 git tag moves last, after both images and the binaries exist. A caller of @v1 never gets a workflow whose image is missing.
  • The images carry the OCI labels source, version, revision and licenses.

docs.title: Which image a workflow runs
docs.text: The reusable workflows and the glassops-platform/glassops action choose their default image from the tag they were called at. A call to @v1 runs the image of the current v1.x.y release, and @v1.2.3 runs the image of v1.2.3. When the reference is a branch or a commit, the image is latest. Pass the image input to override this. For a run you must reproduce exactly, pin a full version or an image digest.

docs.title: Tools in the images
docs.text:
Both images, built from this repository, hold two more programs that GlassOps runs as separate commands:

Program Version Used for cosign v2.5.3 Sigstore signing of PERMITs, when policy.permit.signing is sigstore opa 1.22.0, the static build Rego rules, when policy.rego is set

Both are Apache-2.0 programs copied from their official images, which are pinned by digest in the Dockerfiles. They are not linked into glassops, and they do nothing unless you turn those features on. They are listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES like every other package in the images. The image ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:0.4.0 does not hold them.

docs.title: License scan
docs.text:
Every pull request, every push to main and every release runs the License Scan workflow. It builds both images, writes a software bill of materials for each with syft, and fails when an image holds a package under the AGPL, GPL or LGPL that the allowlist does not list. The release workflow publishes no image unless the scan passes.

How a package is judged:

  • The scan reads the license expression each package declares.
  • In A OR B, one free side is enough, because the user may choose it. In A AND B, both sides must be free.
  • An allowlist line is type:name-glob = license text. It matches only a package whose declared expression equals the text. A package whose license changes comes back into the report.
  • AGPL can never be allowlisted.

The allowlist is scripts/notices/allowlist.txt. It lists the Java runtime of the analyzer image (GPLv2 with the Classpath Exception), and the Alpine base layer packages that the images contain and that GlassOps runs as separate programs, such as git, busybox and coreutils. They are not linked into glassops. The list is reviewed whenever the base image changes.

The scan is an ordinary check and not a required one. Making it required is a branch protection setting.

Run it yourself against an image you built:

scripts/notices/sbom.sh glassops:local glassops.sbom.json
python3 scripts/notices/licenses.py check glassops.sbom.json --allow scripts/notices/allowlist.txt

The second command exits 1 when it finds a package the allowlist does not cover.

docs.title: Third party notices
docs.text:
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES lists the packages in both images with their licenses. The same scan workflow checks that the file still matches what the images contain, and fails when a package was added or removed and the file was not regenerated.

The notices and the project license are inside the images at /usr/share/doc/glassops/, and the release archives include THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES next to LICENSE and README.md:

docker run --rm --entrypoint cat ghcr.io/glassops-platform/glassops:v1 /usr/share/doc/glassops/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES

docs.title: Tested here, and not
docs.text: The tag rules, the license check and the planted-package test run in the workflow license-scan.yml. Pushing a real release tag has not happened with these rules yet, so the sequence of the release workflow on GitHub is untested on a real tag.

docs.title: Sigstore signing
docs.text:
Opt-in, since v1.1.0. HMAC signing stays the default. See what is in which release.

By default a PERMIT is signed with a shared secret, GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY. With Sigstore signing, gate signs the PERMIT keyless on GitHub Actions instead. There is no secret to store or rotate. The signature says which workflow, in which repository, signed the PERMIT, and permit verify and deploy accept only a signature from the workflow and repository you name. The PERMIT itself is unchanged. See PERMIT and rules for what it holds.

GlassOps does not sign anything itself. It runs the separate program cosign, which is in both GlassOps images (see Releases, images and licenses).

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
policy:
  permit:
    signing: sigstore
    identity: https://github.com/acme/sf-app/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@refs/heads/main
    issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
    repository: acme/sf-app
Field Meaning signing hmac (the default) or sigstore identity The certificate identity a signature must carry. Required for sigstore. For GitHub Actions it is https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/.github/workflows/<file>@<full ref>, such as @refs/heads/main or @refs/tags/v1 issuer The OIDC issuer that vouches for the identity. Required for sigstore. For GitHub Actions it is https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com repository The repository, as owner/name, that a signature must come from. On GitHub Actions it defaults to the running repository (GITHUB_REPOSITORY). Off GitHub Actions it is required

glassops doctor and every command that loads the config refuse sigstore without both identity and issuer, and a repository that is not owner/name.

docs.title: What each command needs
docs.text:
gate signs. It stops with exit 2 and writes no PERMIT unless all of these hold, checked in this order:

  1. The run is on GitHub Actions. Bitbucket Pipelines and GitLab CI are not supported for Sigstore signing. Use HMAC there.
  2. The job has an OIDC token. Give the job that runs gate the permission id-token: write. GlassOps checks only that the token variables exist and never reads their values.
  3. cosign is on PATH.
  4. A repository to pin is known.

gate does not read GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY when signing is sigstore.

permit verify and deploy verify. They run cosign verify-blob and accept the PERMIT only when the signature, the transparency log entry and a certificate for the configured identity from the configured issuer, issued to a workflow run in the pinned repository, all check out. Verifying needs no OIDC token, so it works in a job without id-token: write and on a laptop that has cosign. Off GitHub Actions you must set policy.permit.repository. Verifying is refused on Bitbucket Pipelines and GitLab CI. cosign can refresh the Sigstore trust root, so verifying can need network access.

A missing cosign or a missing repository is a tool error (exit 2). A signature that does not verify is a failed check in permit verify (exit 1) and a refusal (exit 2) in deploy, the same as for HMAC. A signature that is not valid base64 or not a cosign bundle is refused before cosign runs. Everything else the PERMIT binds is checked as before: target, commit, plan, config, change set, expiry, lifetime and the clean tree rule.

The signature block of a Sigstore PERMIT has the algorithm sigstore-bundle and no key_id. Its value is the cosign bundle in standard base64. Two bundle shapes are accepted. The one that cosign v2 writes with sign-blob --bundle holds base64Signature, cert and rekorBundle. The newer protobuf bundle carries a mediaType that starts with application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle. Anything else is refused. The images carry cosign v2.5.3.

docs.title: Identity and the repository pin
docs.text:
The certificate identity names the workflow that ran the signing, and it includes the ref that workflow ran at. Two things follow.

Your own workflow. When gate runs in a workflow file in your repository, the identity is that file at that ref, as in the example above. A deploy from main and a deploy from a tag have different identities. Name the one you want to accept, and protect that branch or tag, because anyone who can change the workflow on it can sign.

A reusable workflow. When the signing runs inside a workflow your repository calls, the certificate names the called workflow, not yours. Every repository that calls glassops-deploy.yml@<ref> would share one identity, https://github.com/glassops-platform/glassops/.github/workflows/glassops-deploy.yml@<full ref>. That is why repository exists: the identity alone cannot tell one consumer from another, so verifying also passes --certificate-github-workflow-repository and accepts only a certificate issued to a run in your repository. Do not leave repository out when you set identity to a reusable workflow, and do not rely on identity alone.

The reusable workflow glassops-deploy.yml grants id-token: write to its deploy job and passes the OIDC request variables into the container that runs gate, so a call to it can sign with Sigstore. The caller must grant id-token: write on the job that calls the workflow, because a called workflow cannot hold more than its caller grants. A caller that grants less is refused when the run starts, whichever signing it uses. With HMAC signing the permission goes unused and nothing else changes. glassops doctor recognises a call to the reusable workflow and tells you which identity such a call would carry. You can also run gate in a workflow of your own that grants the permission.

docs.title: What goes into the public log
docs.text: Keyless signing writes to the public Rekor transparency log. Each signing records the SHA-256 of the PERMIT and the signing certificate, never the PERMIT itself. The certificate holds the repository name, the workflow ref and the commit. If your repository is private, its name, the workflow path and the commit hash become public. Anyone can read the log. Use HMAC signing if that is not acceptable.

docs.title: Doctor checks
docs.text:
With policy.permit.signing: sigstore, glassops doctor adds these checks. It adds none for HMAC.

Check What it says tool.cosign Fails when cosign is not found. Otherwise it reports the version permit.sigstore Fails on Bitbucket Pipelines or GitLab CI. On GitHub Actions it passes when the job can request an OIDC token and fails when it cannot. A pull request job without the token gets a warning only. Off any CI it is skipped, because only verifying works there permit.identity Passes with a warning: detail when the issuer is not the GitHub one, when the identity is not shaped like a GitHub workflow identity, or when your workflows call glassops-deploy.yml at a ref the identity does not name permit.repository Reports the repository that will be pinned and where it came from. It warns when none is known, or when the configured one differs from the running repository

docs.title: Tested here, and not
docs.text:
• The signer and verifier are covered by unit tests with a fake cosign, including a wrong identity, a wrong issuer, a wrong repository, a tampered PERMIT, a missing OIDC token, a missing cosign and a non-GitHub CI. Sigstore PERMITs carry and check the same change set and command hashes as HMAC ones.
  • One real signing run on GitHub Actions with cosign v2.5.3 and a dummy file confirmed that cosign finds the job's OIDC token itself, that --bundle writes the older bundle shape, and that the certificate identity is the called workflow and not the caller. That run wrote one public Rekor entry for the dummy file.
  • That a Sigstore signature is produced and verified end to end through a call to the reusable glassops-deploy.yml, and that the pinned repository there is the caller's repository, comes from reading the workflow and cosign's options. It has not been proven on a real run yet.

docs.title: Verify, coverage and YAML settings
docs.text: Settings in glassops.yaml for the post-deploy verify step, for the class coverage check, and the limits the file must stay inside. The schema is schemas/config.json. The exec provider's own settings are on the exec provider page.

docs.title: verify
docs.text:
All keys are optional. See glassops verify for what each check does.

verify:
  smoke: ./ci/smoke.sh
  foreign_deploys: warn
  flows: fail
Key Values Default Meaning verify.smoke a shell command none Runs after verify's own checks, with sh -c in the project directory. Exit 0 passes and any other exit fails verify.foreign_deploys fail, warn, off warn What another deploy to the target during your deploy window does verify.flows fail, warn, off fail What an active Flow that the target does not run as its latest version does

The smoke command gets the usual environment plus GLASSOPS_RESULTS_DIR, GLASSOPS_TARGET and GLASSOPS_TARGET_ID. A command that cannot start is an error.

docs.title: test.coverage.class_scope
docs.text:
test.coverage.class_min fails the test step when any class is below the minimum. sf apex run test lists only the classes a test touched, so a class that no test touched is missing from its answer, and without more help it would never be checked. After a finished test run, GlassOps asks the target for its coverage aggregate and counts the untouched classes at 0%. class_scope says which untouched classes count.

test:
  coverage:
    class_min: 75
    class_scope: changed
Value Classes counted at 0% when no test touched them changed (default) The Apex classes in .glassops/plan.json. With no plan file, every untouched class the target reports, because nothing says which classes changed all The classes in the plan and every untouched class the target reports

Rules that apply to both:

  • A class listed in the plan fact salesforce.apex_nonexecutable_types (changed classes whose top level type is an interface or enum, which have no executable lines) is skipped too. With no such fact in the plan nothing is skipped on that ground.
  • A class listed in the plan fact salesforce.apex_test_classes (changed classes annotated @IsTest) is taken for a test class and skipped. With no such fact in the plan, a class whose name ends in Test is skipped instead. An untouched class that is not in the plan is judged by name, because its source is not read.
  • The classes added this way are recorded in the fact test.coverage_unreported. The provider records the untouched classes it found as test.coverage_untouched.
  • If the coverage aggregate cannot be read, the step fails instead of passing on a missing list. The fact test.coverage_unavailable holds the reason.
  • A plan file that exists and cannot be read fails the step.
  • With class_min or org_min set and no Apex tests found, the step fails, because coverage cannot be checked.

docs.title: YAML limits
docs.text:
glassops.yaml is read as YAML with anchors and aliases allowed, within limits that stop a hostile file from crashing the tool:

  • An alias that refers to itself, directly or through other anchors, is refused. &a [*a] is an error with a line number.
  • The file may not nest deeper than 64 levels.
  • After aliases are expanded, the file may not hold more than 100000 values. An anchor used many times over many levels can reach that, and it is refused instead of expanded.
  • An alias that names no anchor is refused.

A real config is a few hundred values, so none of these limits is reachable by accident. Each refusal is a config error with a message, and the command that loaded the config does not go on.

docs.title: GlassOps examples
docs.text:
consumer/ is the smallest repository layout that runs GlassOps on GitHub. Copy it into a Salesforce DX project, or run glassops init to generate a similar glassops.yaml and workflow.

  • glassops.yaml: two targets, a policy for production, and the default pipelines.
  • .github/workflows/pr.yml: runs the pr pipeline on pull requests by calling the reusable workflow.
  • .github/workflows/deploy.yml: runs the deploy pipeline on a push to main by calling the reusable workflow. The job runs in the glassops-deploy environment.

docs.title: Set up the environment
docs.text:
1. Create the glassops-deploy environment in the repository settings.
  2. Add the required reviewers, and a deployment branch rule that allows main only.
  3. Add GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY as a secret of that environment, not of the repository. Generate the value with openssl rand -base64 32. The deploy workflow passes it by name to the reusable workflow, which resolves it from the environment of the deploy job, because a called workflow gets an environment secret only when the caller passes it.
  4. Add the Salesforce secrets SF_JWT_KEY, SF_CLIENT_ID, SF_USERNAME, SF_DEVHUB_ORG_ID, SF_PROD_USERNAME and SF_PROD_ORG_ID as repository secrets.

The pr workflow never receives the permit key. Only a job in the protected environment can read it. The GitHub deploy guide explains each part of the deploy job.

docs.title: Opt-in policy
docs.text: • rego/: a Rego policy with tests that denies production deploys of protected profiles and permission sets. See Rego rules. Not in a published release yet.

docs.title: Other CI systems
docs.text:
• bitbucket/: bitbucket-pipelines.yml and glassops.yaml for Bitbucket Pipelines.
  • gitlab/: .gitlab-ci.yml and glassops.yaml for GitLab CI.

Neither has run on a real runner yet, so treat the first run as a proof. The Bitbucket and GitLab guide explains what the CI layer reads and writes.

docs.title: Other commands in a workflow
docs.text:
The glassops-platform/glassops action runs one command in the container, for steps that do not fit a pipeline:

- uses: glassops-platform/glassops@v1
  with:
    command: doctor --auth --target prod
    env: |
      SF_JWT_KEY
      SF_CLIENT_ID
  env:
    SF_JWT_KEY: ${{ secrets.SF_JWT_KEY }}
    SF_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.SF_CLIENT_ID }}

docs.title: GlassOps on Bitbucket Pipelines
docs.text:
bitbucket-pipelines.yml runs the pr pipeline on pull requests and the deploy pipeline on a push to main. glassops.yaml is the same Salesforce config as examples/consumer. Copy both into a Salesforce DX project, or run glassops init there.

This layer is written from Atlassian's documentation of the predefined variables. It has not been run on a real Bitbucket runner yet, so treat the first run as a proof.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
1. Enable Pipelines for the repository.
  2. Add the variables glassops.yaml names with $VAR (for example SF_JWT_KEY) as secured repository variables.
  3. Create a production deployment environment, restrict it to main, and add GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY as a secured variable of that environment only. Generate the value with openssl rand -base64 32. The pr pipeline never sees it.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
• The clone is full depth, so change sets between commits are complete.
  • Pull request pipelines report Event as pull_request, with the pull request number and the destination branch.
  • Bitbucket exposes no user name, so the actor is the UUID of whoever started the build.
  • Outputs are appended to .glassops/outputs.env and the run summary to .glassops/summary.md. Both are collected as artifacts. Set GLASSOPS_OUTPUT_FILE or GLASSOPS_SUMMARY_FILE to move them.
  • Approval evidence (labels, environment approvals) is not read from Bitbucket. On this CI, separation of duties is enforce or off per tier.

docs.title: GlassOps on GitLab CI
docs.text:
.gitlab-ci.yml runs the pr pipeline on merge requests and the deploy pipeline on a push to the default branch. glassops.yaml is the same Salesforce config as examples/consumer. Copy both into a Salesforce DX project, or run glassops init there.

This layer is written from GitLab's documentation of the predefined variables. It has not been run on a real GitLab runner yet, so treat the first run as a proof.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
1. Add the variables glassops.yaml names with $VAR (for example SF_JWT_KEY) as masked CI/CD variables.
  2. Protect the default branch. Add GLASSOPS_PERMIT_KEY as a CI/CD variable that is protected, masked and limited to the production environment. Generate the value with openssl rand -base64 32. Merge request pipelines never see it.

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
• GIT_DEPTH: "0" fetches the full history, so change sets between commits are complete.
  • The image sets entrypoint: [""], because GitLab needs a shell to run script lines.
  • Merge request pipelines report Event as pull_request, with the merge request IID and the target branch. Other pipeline sources (schedule, web, api) are passed through as they are.
  • Outputs are appended to .glassops/outputs.env, which the job publishes with artifacts:reports:dotenv. The run summary goes to .glassops/summary.md. Set GLASSOPS_OUTPUT_FILE or GLASSOPS_SUMMARY_FILE to move them.
  • Approval evidence (labels, environment approvals) is not read from GitLab. On this CI, separation of duties is enforce or off per tier.
  • A job token usually cannot push, so moving the glassops/deployed/* tag only warns until you provide a push credential.

docs.title: Rego rules example
docs.text: GlassOps can run your own Rego rules after its built-in rules. This folder holds a small policy that refuses production deploys of protected profiles and permission sets. Rego rules are opt-in and need the opa program on PATH.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
List the Rego files in glassops.yaml. Paths are relative to the project directory.

policy:
  rego:
    files: [policy/deploy.rego]

gate then runs this for the target it checks:

opa eval --format json --input <facts> --data policy/deploy.rego data.glassops.deny

The input is the facts document that gate also writes to .glassops/facts.json:

{
  "schema": "glassops.facts/v1",
  "facts": { "target.tier": "prod", "salesforce.profiles": ["Admin"] }
}

docs.title: Write a rule
docs.text:
Declare package glassops and add entries to the deny set. Each entry is an object with a rule name and a detail text.

deny contains {"rule": "protected_profile", "detail": "the plan changes the Admin profile"} if {
    input.facts["target.tier"] == "prod"
    "Admin" in input.facts["salesforce.profiles"]
}

Each entry becomes a failed check named rego.<rule> in the PERMIT, and any entry denies the deploy. When the set is empty, the PERMIT gets one passing check named rego that names the files and a hash of their contents.

A rule name starts with a letter or digit and holds only letters, digits, _, . and -, up to 100 characters. A detail is cut at 500 bytes, and email addresses in it are masked.

docs.title: What Rego cannot do
docs.text:
• The built-in rules always run first and their results never change. Rego can only add denials. It cannot turn a failed built-in rule into a pass.
  • gate fails closed. When policy.rego is set and opa is missing, a file is missing, opa reports an error, data.glassops.deny is undefined or not a set, or an entry has no valid rule, gate writes a PERMIT that denies and exits 2.
  • A file with the wrong package name leaves data.glassops.deny undefined, so it fails instead of passing quietly.

docs.title: Check it before gate
docs.text:
glassops doctor checks that opa is installed and that the files load and define data.glassops.deny as a set.

Run the tests and try the rules over the two sample inputs, which hold made-up facts:

opa test examples/rego/deploy.rego examples/rego/deploy_test.rego
opa eval --format json --input examples/rego/facts-deny.json --data examples/rego/deploy.rego data.glassops.deny
opa eval --format json --input examples/rego/facts-pass.json --data examples/rego/deploy.rego data.glassops.deny

Name the files for opa test. Passing the whole folder also loads the sample inputs as data, and opa refuses the two because their values conflict.

The facts come from your plan, so a rule can look at the component lists the provider records, such as salesforce.apex_classes, salesforce.permission_sets and salesforce.profiles, and at the target and CI facts such as target.tier, ci.event and ci.labels.
